item.title: Sudden Deaths From Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage and Proximity to Neurosurgical Tertiary Care
item.dc:creator: Aleksanteri Asikainen
Miikka Korja
Jaakko Kaprio
Anna Ranta
Derrick Bennett
Amanda G. Thrift
P. Alan Barber
Suzanne Barker-Collo
item.description:
Authors: Aleksanteri Asikainen, Miikka Korja, Jaakko Kaprio, Anna Ranta, Derrick Bennett, Amanda G. Thrift, P. Alan Barber, Suzanne Barker-Collo, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644245
Abstract: Importance A substantial proportion of deaths due to aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) occur without admission to neurosurgical units. Whether this proportion varies by geographic region is unclear. Objective To determine the proportion of SAH deaths without neurosurgical unit admission across hospital districts in 2 high-income countries. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective, population-based cohort study used 2 externally validated nationwide administrative data collections in all 41 hospital districts and 10 neurosurgical units in Finland and New Zealand from January 1, 2001, to December 31, 2017. Participants included all hospitalized and fatal nonhospitalized cases with SAH. Data were analyzed from July 1, 2024, to September 7, 2026. Exposures Hospital district of residence and its distance to the designated neurosurgical referral center, grouped into 4 zones. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the death-based proportion of all 30-day deaths after SAH that occurred without neurosurgical unit admission (prehospital deaths plus deaths within 30 days after admission to a nonneurosurgical unit divided by all 30-day deaths from SAH). This proportion was estimated across 41 hospital districts and demographic groups, with age- and sex-adjusted risk ratios (RRs) and 95% CIs. Results A total of 12 912 patients with SAH (7856 in Finland and 5056 in New Zealand; median age, 58 [IQR, 49-69] years; 7924 [61.4%] women) were included. Of all 5418 SAH deaths, 3819 (70.5%) occurred without neurosurgical unit admission: 2203 of 3114 (70.7%) in Finland (interdistrict range, 403 of 644 [62.6%] to 5 of 5 [100%]) and 1616 of 2304 (70.1%) in New Zealand (interdistrict range, 111 of 190 [58.4%] to 22 of 23 [95.7%]). Compared with districts containing a neurosurgical unit (1723 of 2602 [66.2%]), the death-based proportions were higher in close-distance (1-130 km; 796 of 1129 [70.5%]; RR, 1.07 [95% CI, 1.02-1.12]), middle-distance (131-157 km; 469 of 599 [78.3%]; RR, 1.18 [95% CI, 1.12-1.24]), and far-distance (158-371 km; 831 of 1088 [76.4%]; RR, 1.15 [95% CI, 1.10-1.20]) zones. This proportion increased by 6.7% (95% CI, 4.9%-8.5%) for each additional 100 km to a neurosurgical unit. The proportions decreased in both countries over time. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of 12 912 patients with SAH, most deaths occurred without neurosurgical unit admission, and this proportion increased with distance to the neurosurgical referral center. Prevention and early management outside tertiary care may therefore warrant priority in reducing SAH mortality.

item.title: Resistance Exercise Training for Depressive Symptoms
item.dc:creator: Darragh O’Sullivan
Jennifer M. Rice
Jacob D. Meyer
Seana Smith
Brett R. Gordon
Cillian McDowell
Ian Sherwin
Mark Lyons
item.description:
Authors: Darragh O’Sullivan, Jennifer M. Rice, Jacob D. Meyer, Seana Smith, Brett R. Gordon, Cillian McDowell, Ian Sherwin, Mark Lyons, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644254
Abstract: Importance Resistance exercise training (RET) has established antidepressant effects compared with inactive control conditions; however, its effects vs active comparisons remain unclear. Objective To quantify the association of RET efficacy with active and inactive comparisons for depressive symptoms and explore variability across moderators. Data Sources Published articles were identified using Google Scholar, MEDLINE, PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycInfo from inception to July 7, 2025. Study Selection Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) with at least 3 weeks of RET or any non-RET comparison and a validated depressive symptom measure at baseline and at least 3 weeks were included. Active comparisons were aerobic exercise training, relaxation, flexibility, mind-body exercise, nutrition, education, advice or attention, mixed activities, and balance exercises. Inactive comparisons were no treatment, waiting lists, and continued usual care. Data Extraction and Synthesis Three reviewers independently extracted data. Meta-regression was used to test moderators, including primary moderators (age, sex, mental health status, RET duration, intensity, concealed allocation). Study quality was assessed using a modified Detsky scale. Main Outcomes and Measures All available associations of RET vs comparison conditions with depressive symptoms were quantified from baseline to at least 3 weeks. Random-effects models were used. Results Across 80 RCTs including 6123 participants (2880 participants [47.0%] in RET groups and 3243 [53.0%] in non-RET comparison groups; mean [SD] age, 57 [16] years; 3412 female [67.1%]), the number of effect sizes examined was 176; 57 RCTs enrolled participants with an illness. Resistance exercise training was associated with a significant, heterogenous, small-magnitude antidepressant effect size (Δ = 0.32 [95% CI, 0.25-0.39]; z = 9.31; P &amp;lt; .001) across all comparisons. The effect size was larger vs inactive comparisons (Δ = 0.54 [95% CI, 0.39-0.68]; z = 7.22; P &amp;lt; .001) than active comparisons (Δ = 0.21 [95% CI, 0.14-0.27]; z = 6.20; P &amp;lt; .001). Versus active comparisons, RET was associated with a significant, heterogenous, small-magnitude antidepressant effect size, with larger effect sizes among participants with a mental illness (Δ = 0.40 [95% CI, 0.29-0.50]) vs without a mental illness (Δ = 0.11 [95% CI, 0.04-0.18]). Versus inactive comparisons, RET was associated with a significant, heterogenous, moderate-magnitude antidepressant effect size, with larger effect sizes for all-female cohorts (Δ = 0.87 [95% CI, 0.60-1.14]), RET frequencies of at least 4 days per week (Δ = 0.46 [95% CI, 0.31-0.60]), and session durations of 30 minutes or less (Δ = 1.75 [95% CI, 0.97-2.54]), and smaller effect sizes with concealed allocation (Δ = 0.32 [95% CI, 0.20-0.44]). Conclusions and Relevance This meta-analysis and meta-regression analysis found that RET was associated with moderate-magnitude, clinically meaningful reductions in depressive symptoms that were greater than other activities with antidepressant benefits, supporting the recommendation of RET in the treatment of depression.

item.title: Neighborhood Exposure to Firearm Violence and Measures of Psychosocial Distress
item.dc:creator: James Macinko
Tanvi Shinkre
Falco J. Bargagli-Stoffi
Jack Kappelman
Diana Silver
item.description:
Authors: James Macinko, Tanvi Shinkre, Falco J. Bargagli-Stoffi, Jack Kappelman, Diana Silver
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644237
Abstract: Importance Exposure to firearm violence is believed to have substantial indirect health effects among those who experience and witness it. Objective To assess whether neighborhood firearm violence is associated with psychological and behavioral outcomes. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study links geocoded, individual-level data from adults participating in the 2021 and 2022 California Health Interview Surveys, a state-representative survey conducted annually by the UCLA Center for Health Policy Research linked to shooting events near interviewees’ home from the Gun Violence Archive. Data analysis was performed from August to October 2025. Exposure Any shooting event occurring within 500 m of interviewees’ households within the past 12 months (January 1, 2020, and December 31, 2022). Sensitivity analyses included any fatal shooting, any shooting within the past 2 months, and more than 1 shooting event. Main Outcome and Measures Primary outcomes were self-reported worry about experiencing firearm violence, feeling unsafe in one’s neighborhood, heavy substance use, and psychological distress. Survey-adjusted multivariable Poisson regression models assessed the association between the exposure and each outcome. Results Among the 45 916 adults interviewed (mean [SD] age, 48.2 [18.7] years; 26 077 [51.8%] female), 6289 (17.2%, weighted) had a shooting occur near their home; there were no missing data. Polysubstance use was positively associated with most exposures, with the highest incident rate ratios (IRRs) among those experiencing a recent shooting in their neighborhood within the past 2 months (IRR, 1.41; 95% CI, 1.18-1.68) and those experiencing more than 1 shooting (IRR, 1.33; 95% CI, 1.14-1.55). The highest magnitude associations for each exposure were observed with the outcome of feeling unsafe in one’s neighborhood among those experiencing a recent shooting event (IRR, 1.73; 95% CI, 1.52-1.97) or more than 1 shooting (IRR, 2.36; 95% CI, 2.17-2.56). All exposures had a positive association with worry about experiencing firearm violence, with IRRs of 1.14 (95% CI, 1.04-1.24) for those experiencing any shooting to 1.28 (95% CI, 1.13-1.43) for those experiencing more than 1 shooting in the past 12 months. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of the association between firearm violence and self-reported psychosocial distress, exposure to neighborhood firearm violence was associated with a range of outcomes that may affect people’s perceptions of their safety and could potentially contribute to negative coping behaviors, such as substance use.

item.title: Climate Vulnerability, Historical Redlining, and Children’s Mental Health Care Use
item.dc:creator: Eun Kyung Lee
Megan B. Cole
Sugy Choi
item.description:
Authors: Eun Kyung Lee, Megan B. Cole, Sugy Choi
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2645085
Abstract: Importance Structural inequities stemming from historical redlining and environmental injustice have created varying levels of risk among marginalized communities. However, the association of climate risk and structural racism with pediatric mental health care use remains underexplored. Objectives To examine associations between climate vulnerability and pediatric mental health care use, and to assess whether these associations vary by historical redlining status. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study of children aged younger than 18 years residing in New York State between 2017 and 2022 used all-payer hospital administrative data from the New York State Department of Health. Statistical analysis was conducted from January 2025 through February 2026. Main Outcome and Measures Outcomes included mental health–related emergency department (ED) and outpatient visits identified using International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision –coded mental health diagnosis subtypes (eg, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), aggregated at the census-tract level. The primary exposure was climate-specific Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles (where 1 indicates low climate vulnerability and 4 indicates high climate vulnerability). Poisson regression models were conducted to examine associations between Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles and mental health–related health care utilization, including interactions with neighborhood-level redlining status (Home Owners’ Loan Corporation grades C/D vs A/B) and subtype-specific analyses. Models adjusted for age, sex, self- or guardian-reported race and ethnicity, and neighborhood-level covariates, with coefficients reported as rate ratios (RRs). Results A total of 553 134 mental health–related visits were included (mean [SD] age, 7.2 [5.8] years; 285 526 male [51.6%]). Compared with children living in areas with the lowest climate vulnerability, those living in the highest-vulnerability areas had higher outpatient visit rates (RR, 1.98; 95% CI, 1.72-2.27) and non–statistically significantly higher ED visit rates (RR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.96-1.35). Associations between high climate vulnerability and mental health–related health care utilization varied by redlining status. In historically redlined neighborhoods, high climate vulnerability was associated with outpatient health care utilization (RR, 1.47; 95% CI, 1.44-1.51; P &amp;lt; .001 for interaction) and, to a lesser extent, ED utilization (RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.02-1.09; P &amp;lt; .001 for interaction); in nonredlined neighborhoods high climate vulnerability was associated with lower outpatient health care utilization (RR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.45-0.49; P &amp;lt; .001 for interaction) and not associated with ED utilization (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.93-1.07). Associations also varied across mental health diagnosis subtypes, with higher climate vulnerability associated with increased health care utilization for most diagnosis subtypes. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of children, residence in historically redlined and climate-vulnerable neighborhoods was associated with higher rates of mental health–related health care utilization. These findings highlight geographic patterns in mental health–related health care utilization that may be relevant to future research on climate preparedness, mental health services, culturally responsive care, and access to services for children experiencing climate-related stressors and structural inequities.

item.title: Multilevel Mobility Intervention and Life-Space Mobility in Older Hospitalized Medical Patients
item.dc:creator: Leon Schiffmann
Pascal Leist
Lisa Marti
Livia Bee
Julia I. Beck
Leandra Pfisterer
Eric Geissbühler
Filippa L. M. Kühni
item.description:
Authors: Leon Schiffmann, Pascal Leist, Lisa Marti, Livia Bee, Julia I. Beck, Leandra Pfisterer, Eric Geissbühler, Filippa L. M. Kühni, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643903
Abstract: Importance Low mobility is common during an acute hospitalization and is associated with adverse outcomes, such as loss of independence and death. Previous interventions that were successful in increasing hospital mobility required resources that are not available in everyday clinical practice, limiting their scalability. Objective To assess whether the theory-informed Intervention to Increase Mobility in Older Hospitalized Medical Patients (INTOMOB) improves life-space mobility at 30 days in older hospitalized medical patients. Design, Setting, and Participants This is a multicenter, parallel, partially blinded, cluster randomized clinical superiority trial, with randomization at the hospital ward level and 180-day follow-up. Patients were recruited between October 2023 and January 2025 at acute general internal medicine wards of 3 Swiss hospitals. Main eligibility criteria were age 60 years or older, living in the community, and planned hospital stay 3 or more days. Intervention The intervention was compared with standard of care and included booklets and videos for patients, health care professional training, and posters in the wards. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was life-space mobility at 30 days, a measure of how far and often a person moves within their environment, from bedroom to beyond their town (range, 0-120 points, with higher scores denoting greater mobility). Secondary outcomes included physical activity during hospitalization, new institutionalizations (ie, transition to nursing home), and quality of life. For time-to-event outcomes, Cox models with cluster-robust SEs were used. Multinomial logistic regression with robust SEs was used for categorical outcomes. Results Of 1334 eligible patients, 383 (median [IQR] age, 75 [68 to 81] years; 234 male [61.1%]) agreed to participate and were randomized to 12 clusters (183 patients [47.8%] in the intervention group and 200 patients [52.2%] in the control group). The primary outcome was available for 327 patients (85.4%). The median (IQR) length of stay was 5 (3 to 7) days. Life-space mobility at 30 days was not significantly different between control and intervention groups (adjusted difference, 0.67 points; 95% CI, −4.35 to 5.68 points). There were no serious adverse events potentially related to the intervention. There was no consistent statistically significant difference in any other secondary outcomes. Conclusions and Relevance The INTOMOB intervention did not result in a significantly improved short-term life-space mobility or other clinical outcomes. However, the feasibility of the INTOMOB intervention provides a foundation for future mobility interventions aiming to improve both effectiveness and applicability in everyday clinical practice. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05639231 ; Swiss National Clinical Trial Portal Identifier: SNCTP000005259

item.title: Study Rationale, Enrollment Characteristics, and Central Review of Clinical Stage
item.dc:creator: Parminder Singh
Melissa Plets
Jason Efsthathiou
Sameer G. Jhavar
Catherine Tangen
Scott Delacroix
Carie Marquette
Kent W. Mouw
item.description:
Authors: Parminder Singh, Melissa Plets, Jason Efsthathiou, Sameer G. Jhavar, Catherine Tangen, Scott Delacroix, Carie Marquette, Kent W. Mouw, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644122
Abstract: Importance Trimodality therapy (TMT) is an established bladder-preservation approach for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). Accurate clinical staging remains challenging and may affect patient selection, trial design, and interpretation of outcomes. Objective To describe the design, accrual, and baseline characteristics of the Phase III Randomized Trial of Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy With or Without Atezolizumab in Localized Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer (INTACT) trial and evaluate agreement between site-reported and centrally reviewed clinical stage and the prevalence of high-risk disease features. Design, Setting, and Participants INTACT is a phase 3 randomized clinical trial that enrolled patients with localized MIBC (stage cT2-T4aN0M0) at 136 US sites between April 2019 and March 2025. For this analysis, 243 patients with available source documentation were randomly selected by the SWOG Statistical Center for central clinical staging review. Interventions Patients were randomized to physician’s choice of concurrent chemotherapy (cisplatin, gemcitabine, or 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin C) and radiotherapy (bladder only or small pelvis; 64-64.8 Gy), with or without atezolizumab (1200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks for 9 cycles). Main Outcomes and Measures The trial’s primary end point is 3-year bladder-intact event-free survival, which is not reported in this analysis. Outcomes for the present analysis included trial accrual, clinical stage distribution, agreement between site-reported stage and the initial independent central reviewer, and prevalence of predefined high-risk features (carcinoma in situ, unilateral hydronephrosis, or tumor &amp;gt;5 cm). Agreement was assessed using Cohen κ and directional disagreement using the McNemar test. Results Among 485 randomized patients, the median (IQR) age was 73.8 (37.6-93.6) years, 384 (79.2%) were male, 16 (3.3%) were Asian, 33 (6.8%) were Black, and 419 (86.4%) were White. Site investigators classified 398 (82.1%) as stage cT2 and 87 (17.9%) as stage cT3 or T4a. Among 243 patients selected for central review, 201 (82.7%) had site-reported stage cT2 disease and 42 (17.3%) had stage cT3 or T4a disease. Agreement between site-reported stage and the initial independent central reviewer was moderate (κ = 0.48; 95% CI, 0.34-0.62). Of 201 site-reported stage cT2 cases, 24 (11.9%) were assigned stage cT3 or T4a by the central reviewer; of 42 site-reported stage cT3 or T4a cases, 15 (35.7%) were assigned stage cT2. Among patients with site-reported stage cT2 disease, 113 (56.2%) had at least 1 high-risk feature. Overall, 155 of 243 patients (63.8%) had at least 1 high-risk feature. Conclusions and Relevance In this phase 3 randomized clinical trial, a pragmatic design facilitated accrual of 485 patients to a US bladder-preservation trial. Clinical staging showed moderate agreement between site investigators and independent central review, and more than half of patients classified as stage cT2 had additional high-risk features. These findings support standardized collection of clinical staging and high-risk disease characteristics in future bladder-preservation trials. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03775265

item.title: Nationwide Assessment of Trends, Characteristics, and Outcomes of Pregnancy for Cancer Survivors
item.dc:creator: Koji Matsuo
Naoko Komura
Aoi Yamaguchi
Yurika Arakaki
Shinya Matsuzaki
Nikita A. Rao
Nandita Ramkumar
Matthew W. Lee
item.description:
Authors: Koji Matsuo, Naoko Komura, Aoi Yamaguchi, Yurika Arakaki, Shinya Matsuzaki, Nikita A. Rao, Nandita Ramkumar, Matthew W. Lee, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644168
Abstract: Importance Cancer survivors are individuals with a diagnosis of malignant neoplasm, either living with (ie, current cancer survivors) or free of (ie, past cancer survivors) cancer. As the prevalence of cancer survivors of reproductive age increases worldwide, assessment of pregnancy characteristics and outcomes among past cancer survivors is important. Objective To assess the temporal trends, clinical and obstetric characteristics, and maternal morbidity at delivery among current and past cancer survivors. Design, Setting, and Participants This nationwide cross-sectional study used National Inpatient Sample data for hospital deliveries from 2016 to 2023. Analyses were conducted from April to May 2026. Exposure A prior or current diagnosis of cancer at hospital delivery, with individuals classified as being a past cancer survivor, a current cancer survivor, or an individual without a cancer diagnosis. Main Outcome and Measure The primary outcome was severe maternal morbidity at delivery, assessed with multivariable generalized linear models with a Poisson distribution. Results Among 28 360 443 hospital deliveries, there were 106 740 (0.4%) hospital deliveries for past cancer survivors, 21 975 (&amp;lt;0.1%) for current cancer survivors, and 28 231 728 (99.5%) without a cancer diagnosis. The median (IQR) maternal age at delivery was 33 (29-36), 32 (27-36), and 29 (25-33) years among past cancer survivors, current cancer survivors, and individuals without a cancer diagnosis, respectively. During the 8-year study period, hospital deliveries for past cancer survivors increased from 30.1 to 45.6 per 10 000 hospital deliveries (average annual percentage change [AAPC] = 6.3% [95% CI, 5.1%-7.9%]), whereas hospital deliveries for current cancer survivors were unchanged (7.0 to 7.4 per 10 000 hospital deliveries; AAPC = 0.2% [95% CI, −2.8% to 3.7%]). Most hospital deliveries (57.6%) for past cancer survivors were full-term, whereas only 39.6% were full-term for current cancer survivors. Compared with the no cancer group, the severe maternal morbidity rate was higher for the past cancer survivor group (11.9 vs 6.8 per 1000 hospital deliveries; adjusted incidence rate ratio [IRR], 1.45 [95% CI, 1.37-1.53]) and for the current cancer survivor group (48.2 vs 6.8 per 1000 hospital deliveries; adjusted IRR, 3.80 [95% CI, 3.58-4.04]), including the inpatient maternal mortality rate during the hospital delivery admission (273.0 vs 7.0 per 100 000 hospital deliveries; adjusted IRR, 14.24 [95% CI, 10.87-18.66]). Conclusions and Relevance In this US cross-sectional study, the prevalence of hospital deliveries for past cancer survivors increased from 2016 to 2023, and severe maternal morbidity was increased at delivery for past and current cancer survivors. These findings support the importance of preconception evaluation for cancer survivors and early referral to tertiary care centers with multidisciplinary teams, as currently recommended by multiple organizations.

item.title: Work Hours, Emergency Department Context, and Workplace Violence Among Nurses
item.dc:creator: Lindsay Thompson Munn
Nathaniel Sean O’Connell
Carolyn S. Huffman
Esita Patel
Kristie L. Foley
Cheryl B. Jones
Jason P. Stopyra
item.description:
Authors: Lindsay Thompson Munn, Nathaniel Sean O’Connell, Carolyn S. Huffman, Esita Patel, Kristie L. Foley, Cheryl B. Jones, Jason P. Stopyra
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644016
Abstract: Importance Workplace violence is common in high-risk health care settings, with consequences for clinician well-being and care delivery. Less is known about multilevel work-system factors associated with workplace violence in emergency department (ED) nurses. Objective To characterize workplace violence among ED nurses and identify multilevel work-system factors associated with workplace violence. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study used nurse survey data combined with administrative and electronic medical record data collected in 2023 from nurses working in 11 EDs in a multisite health system in the southeastern US. Exposure Multilevel work-system factors, with primary exposures of interest including overtime, shift type, and ED type (freestanding vs in-hospital); additional covariates included individual, team, and ED-level characteristics. Main Outcomes and Measures Any self-reported workplace violence in the prior month (threats, physical violence, verbal abuse, unwanted sexual attention, or bullying) from patients, visitors, and/or coworkers. Associations were estimated using mixed-effects logistic regression with a random intercept for emergency department site and factor selection using cross-validated least absolute shrinkage and selectrion operator regression. Nurses in the supplemental staffing team were excluded from this analysis. Results Among 337 ED nurses (mean [SD] age, 34.9 [9.5] years; 289 [85.8%] female; 287 [85.2% white; mean [SD] nursing experience, 9.0 [8.2] years), 296 (87.8%) reported workplace violence in the prior month. Incidents of WPV involved patients or visitors (292 of 296 [98.6%]) and coworkers (60 of 296 [20.3%]). In adjusted mixed-effects models (n = 299), overtime was associated with higher odds of workplace violence (OR, 3.21; 95% CI, 1.30-7.93), while night shift (OR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.10-0.78) and employment in a freestanding ED (OR, 0.25; 95% CI, 0.09-0.76) were associated with lower odds. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of ED nurses, workplace violence was common and was associated with overtime and ED context. These findings support further evaluation of work-hour practices and context-specific approaches to workplace violence prevention.

item.title: Tumor Treating Fields and Quality of Life Among Patients With Locally Advanced Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma
item.dc:creator: Teresa Macarulla
Vincent Picozzi
Sreenivasa R. Chandana
Bohuslav Melichar
Anup Kasi
Jin Gang
Javier Gallego
Christelle de la Fouchardière
item.description:
Authors: Teresa Macarulla, Vincent Picozzi, Sreenivasa R. Chandana, Bohuslav Melichar, Anup Kasi, Jin Gang, Javier Gallego, Christelle de la Fouchardière, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641241
Abstract: Importance The PANOVA-3 trial demonstrated the survival benefit and tolerability of Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields) therapy concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, but understanding the impact of TTFields therapy on quality of life (QoL) and pain is important for clinical decision-making. Objective To analyze the impact of TTFields therapy concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel on QoL and pain outcomes using prospective data from PANOVA-3. Design, Setting, and Participants This is a prespecified secondary analysis of PANOVA-3, which was a global, open-label, multicenter, phase 3 randomized clinical trial in adult patients with previously untreated locally advanced unresectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma (LA-PAC). A total of 571 patients were randomized between May 1, 2018, and March 31, 2023, with follow-up completed October 31, 2024. Data analysis was performed from November 2024 to May 2025. Intervention Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive either TTFields therapy (150 kHz) with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel or gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone. Nab-paclitaxel (125 mg/m 2 ) and gemcitabine (1000 mg/m 2 ) were administered intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of 28-day cycles. Duration of follow-up was 18 months. Main Outcomes and Measures QoL was measured using the European Organization for the Research and Treatment of Cancer Core Quality of Life Questionnaire and the 26-item pancreatic cancer module. End points were mean changes from baseline QoL scores, deterioration-free survival of QoL, and time to opioid use. An analysis of pain medication use was performed post hoc. Results At baseline, 562 patients (median [IQR] age, 67 [31-90] years; 295 [52.5%] female), including 279 of 285 patients in the TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm and 283 of 286 patients in the gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm, completed the EORTC QLQ-C30 questionnaire. Global health status was stable during the 26-month follow-up in both study arms. Digestive symptoms, pain, and pancreatic pain were improved from 2 months after treatment initiation throughout treatment and follow-up in the TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm. TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel was associated with longer deterioration-free survival for global health status than gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone (median [IQR], 7.1 [3.5-14.8] vs 5.7 [2.3-11.5] months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.77; 95% CI, 0.61-0.97; P = .02). Longer deterioration-free survival was also observed for most items on the digestive symptoms scales (indigestion and altered bowel habit were similar between the 2 arms). Median (IQR) deterioration-free survival was significantly longer with TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel for pain (10.1 [4.0-20.9] vs 7.4 [3.5-14.5] months; HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.54-0.89; P = .003) and pancreatic pain (14.7 [6.2-46.2] vs 10.2 [5.6-18.2] months; HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.52-0.90; P = .006) as was median time to opioid use in the modified intention-to-treat population (9.3 [3.9-18.6] vs 6.7 [1.1-16.3] months; HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.55-0.93; P = .01). Conclusions and Relevance This secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial found that TTFields therapy with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel improved QoL and provided clinically meaningful benefits in pain outcomes compared with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone. This study’s results suggest that TTFields therapy with gemicitabine and nab-paclitaxel is practice-changing for patients with unresectable LA-PAC. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03377491

item.title: Penicillin-Cephalosporin Cross-Reactivity Alert Modifications and Cephalosporin Use Among Patients With Untested Penicillin Allergy Labels
item.dc:creator: Cosby A. Stone
Scott D. Nelson
Laura Zahn

Ritu Banerjee

item.description:
Authors: Cosby A. Stone, Scott D. Nelson, Laura Zahn, Allison B. McCoy, Megan Z. Wang, Ritu Banerjee, Milner Staub, Dara Mize, et al.

item.description:
Authors: Molly O. Hunter, Kyulim Lee, Raul E. Sanchez, Isaac Kistler, Charles A. Elmaraghy, Amy M. Manning, Prasanth Pattisapu, Tendy Chiang, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643915
Abstract: Importance Diagnosis and treatment of ankyloglossia has increased in recent years. A lack of universal evaluation and management guidelines may contribute to inconsistent practice patterns and variable access to care. Objective To evaluate access to care and practice pattern variation in the treatment of ankyloglossia as a source of breastfeeding difficulty across clinicians and sites of care in Ohio. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study of pediatric dentists and pediatric and general otolaryngologists providing treatment to pediatric patients in Ohio was conducted using a secret shopper approach from October 6, 2025, to January 5, 2026. All pediatric dentists and otolaryngologists providing treatment to pediatric patients were eligible for inclusion. Health care professionals were identified using lists obtained from the Ohio State Dental Board and the American Academy of Otolaryngology. Exposure Clinics were contacted via phone by a simulated patient’s mother using a vignette describing a 2-week-old infant with breastfeeding difficulty characterized by painful latch and inquiring regarding ankyloglossia (ie, tongue tie) evaluation. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were time to first available appointment and procedure cost to patient on the day of service. Secondary outcomes included referral requirement, potential for same-day procedures, procedure technique, additional procedures discussed during scheduling, insurance acceptance, and total cost of consultation and procedure. Results A total of 175 clinics representing 487 health care professionals (299 dentists and 188 otolaryngologists) were contacted. The median (IQR) appointment wait time was 14 (7-28) days. For practices providing cost information, time-of-service cash payment was required by 31 of 36 dental offices (86%), while all otolaryngology practices (38 of 38; [100%]) billed medical insurance. Dental clinics were more likely to empirically recommend other procedures (eg, maxillary frenulum release) at the time of appointment scheduling (29 of 45 [64%]) than otolaryngology offices (1 of 38 [3%]) ( P &amp;lt; .001). Across all practices, the median (IQR) cost of lingual frenotomy alone was $474 ($350-$545), while total cost (consultation and all recommended procedures) ranged from $200 to $1515. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of pediatric dental and otolaryngology clinics in Ohio, access to care for ankyloglossia was similar, but the anticipated cost of procedures varied widely, as did empiric recommendations for intervention beyond lingual frenotomy. Prospective patients should be aware of this heterogeneity and the potential for significant price differences for treatment.

item.title: Body Mass Index Peak-Rebound Patterns and Inhibitory Control Among Young Children
item.dc:creator: Jamil M. Lane
Izzuddin M. Aris
Hsiao-Hsien Leon Hsu
Emily Oken
Vishal Midya
Rosalind J. Wright
Daniel N. Klein

item.description:
Authors: Jamil M. Lane, Izzuddin M. Aris, Hsiao-Hsien Leon Hsu, Emily Oken, Vishal Midya, Rosalind J. Wright, Daniel N. Klein, María Del Carmen Hernández-Chávez, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642834
Abstract: Importance Childhood obesity has been linked with poor inhibitory control, and atypical body mass index (BMI) growth trajectories may identify children at higher risk for poor inhibitory control. Inhibitory control is also sexually dimorphic (male vs female), as maladaptive inhibitory control is more common in males. Objective To investigate the association between early childhood BMI peak-rebound patterns and inhibitory control development at 4 to 5 and 6 to 7 years and test whether there is a sexually dimorphic association. Design, Setting, and Participants The Programming Research in Obesity, Growth, Environment, and Social Stressors study is a prebirth cohort that recruited pregnant women receiving prenatal care through the Mexican Social Security Institute from July 2007 to February 2010 and followed up from pregnancy through age 8 years. Data were analyzed from November 2024 to December 2025. Exposure Repeated weight and length or height measurements were collected from birth to 8 years and mixed-effects models were used to characterize sex- and child-specific BMI trajectories and derive age and magnitude of the BMI peak (maximum inflection point during infancy) and rebound (minimum inflection point during early childhood). Main Outcomes and Measures Children completed the Conners Kiddie Continuous Performance Test, second edition, to assess inhibitory control at ages 4 to 5 and 6 to 7 years, and linear mixed-effects models were used to assess associations of age and magnitude of BMI peak and rebound with inhibitory control across the 2 time points. Sex-specific trajectories were evaluated by modeling interactions between child sex. Results Among 539 children included in the study, 278 (51.6%) were male; 277 (51.4%) were born to mothers with low socioeconomic status, and the mean (SD) gestational age at birth was 38.4 (1.6) weeks. After adjusting for covariates, a 1-SD higher BMI at peak was associated with higher T-scores for hit reaction time standard errors (β = 0.89; 95% CI, 0.20 to 1.58). A 1-SD higher age at rebound was associated with higher hit reaction time (β = 2.35; 95% CI, −0.01 to 4.72). However, age at peak and BMI at rebound were not associated with any inhibitory control measure. Children with early timing of peak and rebound exhibited higher T-scores for omission errors (β = 4.05; 95% CI, 0.96 to 7.13), while children with early timing of peak and late timing of BMI rebound had lower T-scores for hit reaction time (β = −4.16; 95% CI, −7.29 to −1.02) compared with those with normal timing of peak and rebound. In males, both older age and a higher magnitude of BMI rebound were associated with lower omission error T-scores, whereas in females, variations in age and magnitude of BMI patterns were associated with higher T-scores for hit reaction time and hit reaction time standard errors. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of 539 children in Mexico, early-life BMI peak-rebound trajectories across childhood were associated with inhibitory control. These findings extend the literature beyond the well-established effects of BMI peak-rebound on metabolic conditions.

item.title: Neighborhood Exposome at Birth and Trajectories of Epigenetic Age Acceleration Across Childhood
item.dc:creator: Qingyue E. Yuan
Anne K. Bozack

item.description:
Authors: Qingyue E. Yuan, Anne K. Bozack, Vincent Paquin, Sarina Abrishamcar, Ella J. Arrant, Ying Xu, Sheryl L. Rifas-Shiman, Yinxian Chen, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644321
Abstract: Importance Epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) has been linked to increased disease risk in adults, yet its developmental trajectories and early-life neighborhood determinants remain poorly understood. Objective To examine whether there are associations between the neighborhood exposome at birth and EAA trajectories from early childhood through adolescence. Design, Setting, and Participants This longitudinal cohort study used data from Project Viva, a prebirth cohort that enrolled pregnant women in eastern Massachusetts from April 22, 1999, to July 31, 2002. Participants included 570 children with available peripheral blood DNA methylation data, complete neighborhood characteristics, and complete covariates. Data were analyzed from August 19, 2024, to August 21, 2026. Exposures Neighborhood exposome profiles at birth derived from 22 census tract–level characteristics across 4 domains (area deprivation, social fragmentation, population density, and environmental quality) using self-organizing maps. Main Outcomes and Measures EAA was calculated at 3, 8, and 13 years of age using the Horvath, Skin &amp;amp; Blood, and Wu epigenetic clocks. Trajectories were identified using latent class linear mixed models. Associations between neighborhood profiles and EAA trajectories were estimated using multinomial mixed models. Results Among 570 children (mean [SD] age at early childhood, 3.2 [0.4] years; 305 [53.5%] male), 3 EAA trajectory groups (stable, increasing, and decreasing for the Horvath and Skin &amp;amp; Blood clocks or low-baseline for the Wu clock) and 3 neighborhood profiles were identified. Compared with profile 1 (suburban, lowest adverse exposures [n = 278]), children born into profile 2 (urban, high residential instability and single-person households, and highway proximity [n = 168]) had greater odds of increasing EAA for the Wu clock (adjusted odds ratio, 1.67 [95% CI, 1.03-2.69]). Profile 3 (urban, high socioeconomic deprivation and pollution [n = 124]) showed no associations. Conclusions and Relevance In this longitudinal cohort study, birth into neighborhoods characterized by high residential instability and single-person households and highway proximity was associated with increasing Wu EAA trajectories across childhood. These findings suggest that early-life neighborhood conditions, encompassing both social and physical environmental factors, may represent targets for interventions aimed at reducing long-term disease risk. Further research is needed to clarify the implications of these findings for later health and prevention.

item.title: Racial and Ethnic Differences in County-Level Availability of Uterine Cancer Clinical Trials
item.dc:creator: Ashley S. Felix
Caitlin E. Meade
Jeffrey J. Wing
Simran A. Kanal

Britton Trabert

item.description:
Authors: Ashley S. Felix, Caitlin E. Meade, Jeffrey J. Wing, Simran A. Kanal, Laura M. Chambers, Britton Trabert, Jennifer A. Sinnott
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644045
Abstract: Importance Racial and ethnic disparities exist in clinical trial enrollment, but whether such disparities exist in geographic availability of uterine cancer trials is unknown. Objective To examine associations between race and ethnicity and county-level presence and rates of available uterine cancer clinical trials. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study linked Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Research Plus; Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov; and American Community Survey data of adult patients (aged ≥18 years) diagnosed with uterine cancer between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2021. The data analysis was performed between November 10, 2025, and September 9, 2026. Exposures Race and ethnicity categorized as American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black, Hispanic (any race), Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and White. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcomes were county-level presence and rate of interventional uterine cancer trials. Hurdle models were used to estimate racial and ethnic differences in the odds of residing in a county with at least 1 trial and among patients in counties with trial availability, differences in rates of trials per person. Models accounted for county clustering and were adjusted for patient characteristics. Results Among 155 811 patients in the cohort (median [IQR] age at diagnosis, 62 [55-69] years; 1055 identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native [0.7%], 12 753 as Asian [8.2%], 16 303 as Black [10.5%], 23 177 as Hispanic [14.9%], 2175 as Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander [1.4%], and 100 348 as White [64.4%] race and ethnicity), 121 525 (78.0%) resided in a county with at least 1 available trial. Trial availability was observed among 58.0% of American Indian or Alaska Native patients, 94.3% of Asian patients, 77.7% of Black patients, 86.1% of Hispanic patients, 90.3% of Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander patients, and 74.1% of White patients. Compared with White patients, higher odds of residing in counties with at least 1 available trial were found for Asian (odds ratio [OR], 5.83; 95% CI, 4.83-7.12), Black (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.07-1.30), Hispanic (OR, 2.18; 95% CI, 1.80-2.63), and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (OR, 3.34; 95% CI, 2.17-5.66) patients, whereas American Indian or Alaska Native patients had lower odds (OR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.39-0.61). Among patients in counties with at least 1 trial, fewer available trials per person were found for Asian (rate ratio [RR], 0.69; 95% CI, 0.65-0.74), Hispanic (RR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.52-0.61), and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (RR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.80-0.95) patients compared with White patients. Conclusions and Relevance This cohort study of patients with uterine cancer found that racial and ethnic patterns in geographic trial availability differed by how availability was measured. The presence of any trial may not fully capture geographic access to clinical trial opportunities.

item.description:
Authors: Stephanie A. S. Staras, Carma L. Bylund, Matthew J. Gurka, Lindsay A. Thompson, Marta D. Hansen, Tuo Lin, Pengchen Wang, Gabriela Sanchez, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642247
Abstract: Importance Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination rates among adolescents remain below recommendations. Objective To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician communication training and parent-targeted text messages at increasing HPV vaccination among children aged 11 to 12 years. Design, Setting, and Participants This doubly randomized, 2-level nested clinical trial was conducted from February 2022 to September 2024 among clinicians at 30 pediatric primary care clinics in Florida, children aged 10 to 12 years who had not received any of the 3 adolescent HPV vaccines, and their parents. Interventions occurred for 1 year, and vaccine records were collected for 2 years. Interventions Clinics were randomized 1:1:1 to 3 training groups: (1) the bundled approach, which presents the HPV vaccine in the middle of 2 other recommended vaccines; (2) the focused approach, which emphasizes cancer prevention; and (3) deferred, which offered clinicians the opportunity to participate in the focused training after the trial concluded. Clinicians in the first 2 groups completed a 1-hour communication training and a 5-minute booster session. Patients within clinics were randomized 1:1:1 to 3 text message groups, aligned with the communication strategies: (1) bundled, (2) focused, and (3) no text messages. Parents were sent text messages at the start of the study or prior to their child’s 11th birthday as well as prior to appointments. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were HPV vaccine initiation (receipt of first dose) and completion (receipt of second dose). Analyses accounted for clinic-level clustering. Effects were analyzed as randomized and text messages as received. Results At baseline, 59 clinicians (44 [75%] female; 12 [20%] Asian, 21 [36%] Hispanic, and 21 [36%] non-Hispanic White) within 30 randomized clinics were included, with 17 randomized to the focused group, 21 to the bundled group, and 21 to the deferred group. A total of 7234 children were aged 10 (3576 [49%]), 11 (2617 [36%]), and 12 (1041 [14%]) years at study start (1673 [23%] Hispanic, 1001 [14%] non-Hispanic Black, and 1210 [17%] non-Hispanic White). A total of 28 clinics (93%), 50 clinicians (85%), and 6498 children (90%) completed the 2-year follow-up. The mean pre-post clinic-level difference for HPV vaccine initiation was 28.2 (95% CI, 25.3-31.1) percentage points and for completion was 16.1 (95% CI, 13.3-18.9) percentage points. Risk ratios for clinician training and text messaging did not differ between groups for initiation or completion. Among patients whose parents received text messages vs not, the risk ratio for initiation was 1.17 (95% CI, 1.08-1.26) and for completion was 1.29 (95% CI, 1.06-1.56). Conclusions and Relevance In this study of Florida children aged 10 to 12 years, clinic-level HPV vaccination increased over time. No differences in HPV vaccination by random assignment of clinician training or text messages were detected. When received, text messages were associated with higher HPV vaccination. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05006833

Bonnie Zapolin

item.description:
Authors: Abigail Wilpers, Bonnie Zapolin, Katie Francis, Amy B. Powne, Isha Suba, Dana Zapolin, John Abdelshaheed, Jasmine Mohanlall, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642991
Abstract: Importance Maternal-fetal surgery has expanded rapidly in the US, but how insurance coverage supports delivery of this specialized, high-cost care has not been systematically characterized. Objective To characterize publicly ascertainable information about how Medicaid programs and large commercial insurers cover procedures used in maternal-fetal surgery. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional descriptive study analyzed insurance coverage policies in the US from March through August 2025. Medicaid programs and large commercial insurers were selected based on national market share. Exposure Insurance coverage policies for maternal-fetal surgery–related procedures were assessed using publicly available fee schedules and structured outreach to payer representatives. Main Outcomes and Measures Coverage status (covered, not covered, or data not available) for 19 maternal-fetal surgery–related Current Procedural Terminology ( CPT ) and Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System (HCPCS) codes and 5 comparator codes. Results The study included 50 state Medicaid programs and 30 large commercial insurers. Among Medicaid programs, coverage was high for nonspecific or individual components of procedures (eg, intrauterine transfusion: 49 of 49 available determinations [100%]) but incomplete and highly variable for codes specific to comprehensive interventions (eg, 6 of 36 available determinations [16.7%] for in utero sacrococcygeal teratoma resection). Among 44 states with available determinations for both code types, mean (SD) coverage was higher for CPT codes than S-codes (86.3% [14.1%] vs 53.0% [37.0%]; P &amp;lt; .001), with consistent findings in sensitivity analyses. The median (range) proportion of MFS-related codes covered per state was 14.5 (0-19) of 19 codes (76.3%). Among 5 commercial insurers with data, all 5 (100.0%) reported coverage of all 4 S-codes representing comprehensive interventions. Conclusions and Relevance In this study, coverage of maternal-fetal surgery–related codes was incomplete and variable, and transparency in commercial coverage policies was limited. These findings suggest that coverage uncertainty may complicate health-system planning and financing for this increasingly used, high-cost care.

item.title: Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities in Preschoolers With Bilateral Cerebral Palsy
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Araneda
Daniela Ebner-Karestinos
Julie Paradis
Geoffroy Saussez
Josselin Demas
Rodolphe Bailly
Sandra Bouvier

item.description:
Authors: Rodrigo Araneda, Daniela Ebner-Karestinos, Julie Paradis, Geoffroy Saussez, Josselin Demas, Rodolphe Bailly, Sandra Bouvier, Astrid Carton de Tournai, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643492
Abstract: Importance Intensive interventions for children with cerebral palsy (CP) have traditionally focused on the upper extremities, despite frequent impairments in gross motor function and the critical period of motor development occurring before age 5 years. Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities (HABIT-ILE) has demonstrated efficacy in improving manual dexterity and gross motor function in school-aged children, but evidence in preschool children with bilateral CP remains limited. Objective To determine whether early HABIT-ILE improves gross motor function more than usual unstructured motor activities in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter randomized clinical trial was conducted between December 2019 and December 2021. Recruitment was from European university hospitals, CP-specialized centers, and spontaneous applications at 4 sites: Brussels, Belgium; Brest and Angers, France; and Pisa, Italy. Children aged 12 to 59 months with spastic or dyskinetic bilateral CP who were able to follow instructions were included. Exclusion criteria were uncontrolled seizures, scheduled botulinum toxin injections or orthopedic surgery during the 6 months before or during the study period, severe visual or cognitive impairments, and contraindications to magnetic resonance imaging. Data were analyzed in May 2024. Interventions Children were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive 2 weeks of usual motor activity, including usual rehabilitation (control group), or 2 weeks (50 hours) of HABIT-ILE (HABIT-ILE group). Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was Gross Motor Function Measure-66 (GMFM-66; range, 0-100, with lower scores indicating lesser gross motor ability). Secondary outcomes included Both Hand Assessment (BoHA), Melbourne Assessment 2, Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory-Computer Adaptive Test (PEDI-CAT), and Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM). Assessments were performed at baseline (immediately before intervention) and 2 weeks and 3 months after baseline. Results Among 49 preschool children with CP (mean [SD] age, 40.18 [11.53] months; 18 girls [36.7%] and 31 boys [63.3%]), Gross Motor Function Classification levels were I in 5 children, II in 14 children, III in 17 children, and IV or V in 13 children and Mini-Manual Ability Classification levels were I in 10 children, II in 27 children, III in 7 children, and IV or V in 6 children. Change in mean (SD) GMFM-66 score from baseline to 3 months was significantly greater in the HABIT-ILE group (5.01 [2.52] logits) than the control group (0.70 [1.98] logits) (adjusted mean difference [aMD] in score, 4.33 logits; 95% CI, 3.03-5.62 logits; P &amp;lt; .001). Likewise, mean (SD) scores favored the HABIT-ILE group vs the control group for secondary outcomes of BoHA (5.32 [4.47] vs 0.13 [5.16]; aMD, 5.15; 95% CI, 2.23-8.08; P &amp;lt; .001), PEDI-CAT mobility domain (1.70 [2.18] vs −0.40 [4.38]; aMD, 2.27; 95% CI, 0.20-4.33; P = .03), and COPM performance (4.22 [1.61] vs 1.14 [1.35]; aMD, 3.55; 95% CI, 2.86-4.24; P &amp;lt; .001) and satisfaction (4.37 [1.38] vs 1.15 [1.63]; aMD, 3.11; 95% CI, 2.25-3.97; P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial, early HABIT-ILE significantly improved upper and lower extremities motor performance in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP at 3 months after the intervention. These findings suggest that HABIT-ILE is effective in improving gross motor function in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP. Trial Registration Clinicaltrial.gov Identifier: NCT04020354

item.description:
Authors: Laurie A. Lee, Jennifer R. Foster, Karla D. Krewulak, Dana Rhyno, Molly J. Ryan, Corey Slumkoski, Martha Walls, Neda Zafranchi-Moghadam, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643825
Abstract: Importance Family presence supports critically ill children, yet pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) policies remain inconsistent, creating inequities in access to parents or caregivers. Clear guidance is needed to support equitable, child-centered policy development. Objective To generate evidence-informed and knowledge user–informed recommendations for family presence policies in PICUs. Design, Setting, and Participants This survey study, conducted through surveys and virtual meetings, used a modified Delphi consensus process. Candidate items were derived from family presence guidance documents and PICU family presence research (environmental scan; scoping review; surveys and interviews with patients, families, and health care professionals; and focus groups). Items were organized into themes covering policy priorities; policy-making responsibilities; baseline and emergency policies; and policy communication, enforcement, and revision. From February 2024 to February 2025, panelists completed 2 rating rounds and 1 virtual meeting, with follow-up meetings and member-checking to incorporate input across knowledge user groups. Knowledge users included former PICU patients, family members, clinicians, and policymakers (hospital and PICU administrators and infection prevention and control specialists) from across Canada. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcome was consensus-derived policy priorities and recommendations for PICU family presence during baseline operations and emergency situations. Results Forty-three knowledge users, including 5 patients, 12 family members, 21 clinicians, and 5 policymakers (35 self-reported women or girls [81.4%]), agreed on 10 policy priorities and 44 recommendations. Key messages included that children should be at the center of policy-related decision-making and always have access to at least 2 primary caregivers; families should determine sibling presence and assume responsibility for it; policies should recognize the importance of visitors beyond family for the child’s well-being; and policies should be flexible, adapting to different situations while adhering to core priorities. Recommendations addressed who should make policies; communication, enforcement, and change processes; number, type (eg, parents or caregivers, siblings, and visitors), and timing of bedside presence; family movement and supports; and approaches to personal protective equipment and infectious symptoms to preserve family presence, including during emergencies. Conclusions and Relevance This survey study with consensus-based recommendations for PICU family presence provided a framework for policy design in routine and emergency contexts. The recommendations emphasized the patient’s best interest and continued access to at least 2 primary caregivers. They supported context-specific and unit-specific policy design and may be broadly applicable across children’s hospitals.

item.title: Procalcitonin- and Presepsin-Guided Antibiotics for Early-Onset Sepsis in Preterm Infants

item.description:
Authors: Carlo Dani, Chiara Poggi, Carlo Pietrasanta, Camilla Cattaneo, Monica Fumagalli, Massimo Agosti, Simona Perniciaro, Marcello Napolitano, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643418
Abstract: Importance Early administration of antibiotics in the absence of proven sepsis, such as for treatment of early-onset sepsis (EOS), has been associated with adverse outcomes in very preterm infants. Reference values for procalcitonin (PCT) and presepsin (P-SEP) have been established in preterm infants. Objective To determine whether PCT- and P-SEP–guided antibiotic treatment for EOS was noninferior to universal antibiotic treatment with respect to survival without major morbidity. Design, Setting, and Participants This randomized multicenter noninferiority clinical trial was conducted in 17 Italian neonatal intensive care units between June 1, 2023, and January 31, 2025, among preterm infants born at 25 weeks and 0 days to 31 weeks and 6 days of gestation. Interventions Enrolled infants were randomly allocated to receive either PCT- and P-SEP–guided antibiotic treatment, administered if PCT and P-SEP levels exceeded prespecified thresholds, or universal antibiotic treatment for EOS. Main Outcomes and Measures The composite primary outcome was defined as survival without late-onset sepsis (LOS), bronchopulmonary dysplasia, grade 3 or 4 intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), grade 2 or higher necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), or stage 3 or higher retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). The prespecified noninferiority margin was −5 percentage points. Both a primary intention-to-treat analysis and a secondary per-protocol analysis were performed, as recommended for noninferiority trials. Results The study enrolled and randomized 283 very preterm infants (mean [SD] gestational age, 30.2 [2.2] weeks; 161 girls [57%]); 143 received procalcitonin- and presepsin-guided treatment and 140 received universal antibiotic treatment. The primary outcome did not differ between the PCT- and P-SEP–guided treatment group and the universal antibiotic treatment groups (76 of 143 [53%] vs 77 of 140 [55%]; risk difference, −1.8 percentage points; 90% CI, −11.9 to 8.3 percentage points; P = .32). Noninferiority of PCT- and P-SEP–guided treatment compared with universal treatment was not demonstrated, because the lower bound of the 2-sided 90% CI crossed the prespecified noninferiority margin. The risk differences for LOS, IVH, NEC, PVL, ROP, and death were not significantly different between the groups. PCT and P-SEP values were not different between the groups. No patient developed EOS. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial conducted among neonates born between 25 weeks and 0 days and 31 weeks and 6 days of gestation, a PCT- and P-SEP–guided strategy for the treatment of EOS did not demonstrate noninferiority to universal antibiotic treatment with respect to survival without major morbidity. Within the limits of this study, these findings do not support the routine use of a biomarker-guided approach as an alternative to universal treatment for this high-risk population. Trial Registration Clinicaltrials.gov identifier: NCT05796115

Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643815
Abstract: Importance Patients with celiac disease (CD) may face elevated risk of eating disorders, potentially due to genetic susceptibility and psychosocial factors of a gluten-free diet. However, up-to-date population-based evidence is scarce, and whether any excess risk extends to biological first-degree relatives (bFDRs) remains unclear. Objective To investigate the risk of eating disorders in patients with CD and their bFDRs, including parents, full siblings, and offspring. Design, Setting, and Participants A nationwide multigenerational cohort study of patients with celiac disease in Sweden, observed from January 2002 to December 2023. Data were analyzed from December 2025 to August 2026. From Sweden’s 28 histopathology departments, patients with biopsy-confirmed CD diagnosed 2002 to 2023 were identified. Each patient was matched with fewer than or equal to 5 general population reference individuals; bFDRs of patients with CD and reference individuals were also identified. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was any eating disorder. The adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) for eating disorders diagnosed at age 6 years or older were estimated using Cox regression and flexible parametric survival models for the overall and time-varying estimates, respectively. Results This study included 37 853 patients with CD (23 704 [62.6%] female; median [IQR] age at index date 28.7 [11.7-53.0] years ) and 185 159 reference individuals. Over 10.9 years median follow-up (IQR, 5.9-15.8 years), 485 patients with CD and 1578 reference individuals were diagnosed with any eating disorder. CD was associated with an increased hazard for eating disorders (aHR, 1.39; 95% CI,1.27-1.53), most apparent during the first 5 years of follow-up. Over 20 years of follow-up, 1 extra eating disorder case was expected per 222 patients with CD. In contrast, there was no hazard elevation for any eating disorder among CD-bFDRs (53 435 parents: aHR, 0.82 [0.61-1.12]; 48 743 siblings: aHR, 1.11 [0.99–1.24]; 38 695 offspring: aHR, 1.05 [0.92-1.20]). Sensitivity analyses mitigating information bias and residual confounding largely aligned with main findings. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of patients with CD, a moderately increased eating disorders risk particularly during the first 5 years of follow-up was observed, although the absolute risk was low. This increased risk did not extend to bFDRs of patients with CD. Clinical vigilance toward disordered eating is important among patients with newly diagnosed CD.

item.title: Cumulative Stress and Health Care Utilization Among US Service Members
item.dc:creator: Daniel F. López-Cevallos
Claire A. Kolaja
Edward Chauca
Scott C. Roesch
Neika Sharifian
Felicia R. Carey

Sheila F. Castañeda
item.description:
Authors: Daniel F. López-Cevallos, Claire A. Kolaja, Edward Chauca, Scott C. Roesch, Neika Sharifian, Felicia R. Carey, Matthew A. Allison, Sheila F. Castañeda, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643810
Abstract: Importance Military personnel experience unique occupational stressors, which, combined with other life stressors, may substantially impact their health readiness. Stress exposure is known to be associated with health and health care concerns in civilian populations, but little is known as to whether these associations are present among US service members. Objective To evaluate the association between individual stressors, cumulative stress exposure, and health care utilization (HCU) among a contemporary sample of US service members. Design, Setting, and Participants This prospective cohort analysis used self-reported survey data from the Millennium Cohort Study and up to 3 years of inpatient and outpatient HCU data from Military Health System electronic health records (2020-2023) from US active-duty service members who first completed a Millennium Cohort Study baseline survey in 2020 and 2021. Data were analyzed from January to May 2026. Exposure Self-reported stress exposure (adverse childhood experiences, stressful life events, discrimination, bullying, hazing, and combat experiences) was assessed in 2020 and 2021. Main Outcomes and Measures Inpatient, outpatient, and total HCU patient-days were calculated. Negative binomial regression models examined the HCU association with cumulative and individual stress exposures, adjusting for demographic and military characteristics. Results A total of 34 731 service members were included in the analytic sample (33 252 [95.8%] were young adults aged 17-34 years; 9906 [28.5%] were female). They spent a mean (SD) of 17.74 (19.10) days (median [IQR], 12 [2-23] days) in outpatient and 0.61 (4.98) days (median [IQR], 0 [0-0] days) in inpatient care across a mean (SD) follow-up period of 2.08 (0.84) years. Higher cumulative stress exposure was associated with greater total (incidence rate ratio [IRR], 1.54; 95% CI, 1.50-1.57), inpatient (IRR, 2.28; 95% CI, 2.21-2.35), and outpatient (IRR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.47-1.54) HCU. Individual stressors, particularly adverse childhood experiences and stressful life events, were also associated with greater HCU. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of contemporary US active-duty service members, increased stress exposure was positively associated with greater HCU. Identifying and triaging various stress exposures during outpatient visits can support better access to inpatient care for service members. In turn, these efforts may translate into better patient outcomes, medical readiness, and military health system improvements.

item.title: Civil Society Organization–Led Home Visit Intervention to Reduce Unintentional Child Injury in Rural China
item.dc:creator: Pan Wen
Ziyue Tan
Jing Zhuang
Xiaodong Chen
Xiujuan Li
Yaogui Lu
Liping Li
item.description:
Authors: Pan Wen, Ziyue Tan, Jing Zhuang, Xiaodong Chen, Xiujuan Li, Yaogui Lu, Liping Li
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643140
Abstract: Importance Unintentional injuries are a leading cause of childhood death and disability, but evidence on scalable home visit interventions in rural settings is limited. Objective To evaluate whether a civil society organization–led home visit intervention can reduce unintentional injuries among children and improve caregiver and household safety. Design, Setting, and Participants This outcome assessor–blinded cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 24 rural communities in Guizhou and Shaanxi, China, from May 6 to October 1, 2025. After baseline assessment, communities were randomized as clusters in a 1:1 ratio. Participants were households with children aged 3 to 12 years. Interventions Control communities received routine social worker home visits; intervention communities received routine services plus 3 monthly structured visits with home safety and first aid tool kits and a follow-up visit at month 4. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was caregiver-reported cumulative child unintentional injury incidence during 4 months, a subjective outcome with caregivers unblinded to group allocation. Secondary outcomes were caregiver knowledge, safety attitudes, and supervisory behaviors, with scores ranging from 0 to 40, 0 to 8, and 0 to 80, respectively, with higher scores indicating better knowledge, more positive safety attitudes, and more appropriate supervisory behaviors, respectively, and household environmental hazards, with scores ranging from 0 to 230 and higher scores indicating more household environmental hazards and a less safe home environment. Generalized estimating equations accounted for clustering. Results Among 24 randomized clusters, caregivers (mean [SD] age, 45.4 [13.0] years; 271 [75.3%] female) and children (mean [SD] age, 8.6 [2.3] years, 198 [55.0%] female) from 360 households were enrolled, with 180 each randomized to intervention and control groups. After baseline, 9 households withdrew with missing outcome data; all 360 households were included in the intention-to-treat analyses with multiple imputation. Injury occurred in 21 of 178 households (11.8%) with observed outcomes in the intervention group and 33 of 173 (19.1%) in the control group. The intervention was associated with lower injury odds (adjusted odds ratio, 0.36 [95% CI, 0.18-0.73]; P = .005). At month 4, adjusted mean differences favored the intervention for supervisory behaviors (17.08 [95% CI, 14.71-19.46] points) and household environmental hazards (−36.66 [95% CI, −42.87 to −30.46] points). Conclusions and Relevance In this cluster randomized clinical trial of households with children aged 3 to 12 years, a civil society organization–led home visit intervention reduced caregiver-reported unintentional injuries and improved caregiver supervisory behaviors and household safety during the 4-month intervention period. Longer follow-up is needed to assess durability of the response. Trial Registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry Identifier: ChiCTR2500098928

item.dc:creator: Alison Reid
Amina Tran
Suparna Thakali
Daniel Wetterskog
Francesco Orlando
Anna Wingate
Priyanka Patel

item.description:
Authors: Alison Reid, Amina Tran, Suparna Thakali, Daniel Wetterskog, Francesco Orlando, Anna Wingate, Priyanka Patel, Aidan Cole, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643400
Abstract: Importance Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is increasingly used for oligoprogressive prostate cancer, but the duration of disease control is highly variable. Objective To evaluate time to progression based on circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) prior to SBRT. Design, Setting, and Participants Between October 17, 2018, and February 1, 2023, the phase 2 prospective, single-arm, nonrandomized clinical TRAP (Targeted Radiotherapy in Androgen-Suppressed Prostate Cancer Patients) trial evaluated SBRT to treat 81 patients with castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and 2 or fewer metastases and imaging evidence of progression while receiving an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI). Plasma DNA was collected at 1 or 2 points prior to SBRT and centrally tested for ctDNA using the next-generation sequencing assay PCF_SELECT. Data were collected prospectively using electronic trial case report forms. Data were extracted November 26, 2025. The median follow-up was 24.5 (IQR, 23.7-36.3) months. Exposures Progressing metastases were treated with SBRT, and patients were followed up with clinical assessments, serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) tests, and imaging. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome measure was time to progression, defined as an increase in serum prostate-specific antigen level of 25% or greater from the post-SBRT nadir, radiologic or symptomatic progression, clinician decision to stop ARPI, or death from any cause. The secondary outcomes were time to next therapy or death from any cause. All end points were measured from time of final SBRT treatment. Results Of 77 patients with evaluable blood samples taken prior to SBRT, 19 (24.7%) were in the ctDNA-positive group. The 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate was 21.1% (95% CI, 6.6%-41.0%) for the ctDNA-positive group compared with 58.3% (95% CI, 44.5%-69.8%) for the ctDNA-negative group. The median PFS was 3.0 (95% CI, 2.7-5.9) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 7.8 (95% CI, 5.9-11.4) months for the ctDNA negative group (log rank test, P = .003 at 5% significance level). The median time to initiation of a new therapy or death was 15.3 (95% CI, 4.7-26.0) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 29.6 (95% CI, 17.8-37.6) months for the ctDNA-negative group. The median overall survival was 27.2 (95% CI, 19.2 to undefined) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 33.6 (95% CI, 28.4-38.2) months for the ctDNA-negative group. Conclusions and Relevance These findings suggest that for patients with oligoprogression and no ctDNA, SBRT and continued ARPI could be considered a valid option for prolonging disease control. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03644303

item.title: Importance of Angina Pectoris by Coronary Artery Disease Severity
item.dc:creator: Kerstin Welén Schef
Christian Dworeck
Nina Johnston
Sofia Sederholm Laweson
Stefan Söderberg
Per Tornvall
Moman Aladdin Mohammad
Tomas Jernberg
item.description:
Authors: Kerstin Welén Schef, Christian Dworeck, Nina Johnston, Sofia Sederholm Laweson, Stefan Söderberg, Per Tornvall, Moman Aladdin Mohammad, Tomas Jernberg
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643292
Abstract: Importance Angina pectoris remains a common clinical manifestation, but contemporary population-based data on its long-term prognostic significance are limited. Objective To evaluate the long-term importance of angina pectoris in association with coronary artery disease (CAD) severity determined by coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) in a general population. Design, Setting, and Participants This population-based cohort study included participants from the Swedish Cardiopulmonary Bioimage Study who had completed the Rose Questionnaire and underwent valid CCTA from November 2013 to October 2018, excluding participants with prior myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure, or coronary revascularization. Follow-up continued through September 2024. Data analyses were conducted between August 2025 and January 2026. Exposures Angina (defined by the Rose Questionnaire) and CAD (categorized as no findings, nonobstructive CAD [&amp;lt;50% stenosis], or obstructive CAD [≥50% stenosis]) according to CCTA findings. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was MI or coronary death. The secondary outcome was major adverse cardiac events (MACE), defined as MI, coronary revascularization, heart failure hospitalization, or death from coronary disease or heart failure. Associations were evaluated using Cox regression with sequential multivariable adjustment and stratification by CAD category and presented as hazard ratios (HRs). Results This study included 24 176 individuals (median [IQR] age, 57 [54-61] years; 12 225 female [50.6%]; 1615 with hyperlipidemia [6.8%]; 4374 with hypertension [18.3%]; 703 with diabetes [2.9%]). Angina was present in 720 participants (3.0%). During a median (IQR) follow-up of 7.7 (6.9-8.6) years, 293 primary events occurred. Angina was associated with a higher incidence of MI or coronary death compared with no angina (21 participants [2.9%] vs 272 participants [1.2%]; HR, 2.50; 95% CI, 1.60-3.90). Event rates increased across CAD categories, with no evidence of interaction between angina and CAD severity. After multivariable adjustment, angina remained independently associated with the primary outcome (HR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.04-2.63). Similar associations were observed for MACE (adjusted HR, 2.34; 95% CI, 1.73-3.16). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of a contemporary general population, angina pectoris was associated with adverse cardiac outcomes, independent of CAD severity assessed by CCTA. These findings suggest that symptom assessment remains relevant in cardiovascular risk stratification because it provided incremental prognostic information that may reflect underlying coronary microvascular dysfunction or vasomotor disorders.

item.title: Avoidable Mortality in Adults With Down Syndrome or With Other Intellectual Disabilities
item.dc:creator: Lili Bokor
Michael Kwan Leung Yu
Ben Carter
Umesh Chauhan
Rory Sheehan
André Strydom
item.description:
Authors: Lili Bokor, Michael Kwan Leung Yu, Ben Carter, Umesh Chauhan, Rory Sheehan, André Strydom
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643229
Abstract: Importance Down syndrome is the most common genetic cause of Alzheimer disease. Adults with Down syndrome experience higher mortality than the general population. However, the avoidable causes and their associated factors remain unclear. Objective To compare the proportion and causes of avoidable mortality in adults with Down syndrome, adults with other intellectual disabilities, and the general population, and to identify factors associated with avoidable death. Design, Setting, and Participants This population-based retrospective cohort study used data from the Learning From Lives and Deaths mortality review and the Office for National Statistics in England from 2016 to 2023. It included adults with Down syndrome (n = 3381), other adults with intellectual disabilities (n = 15 347), and the general population (n = 4 163 160). Exposures Down syndrome status, ethnicity, socioeconomic deprivation, co-occurring health conditions, COVID-19 pandemic period. Main outcomes and measures Proportion and causes of avoidable, treatable, and preventable deaths according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development/Eurostat criteria; odds of avoidable death estimated using logistic regression; and age at avoidable death using Cox regression. Factors associated with avoidable death and age at death were also evaluated. Results Among 3381 adults with Down syndrome (1892 male [56.0%]; median [IQR] age at death, 59.5 [54.3-64.2] years), 1589 (47.0%) died from avoidable causes. Among 15 347 adults with other intellectual disabilities (8675 male [56.5%]; median [IQR] age at death, 63.8 [51.7-73.4] years), 6885 (44.9%) died from avoidable causes. Both proportions were substantially higher than in the general population (22.0%) (both P &amp;lt; .001). Treatable deaths were more common (972 [28.7%] vs 3847 [25.1%] vs 317 968 [7.6%]), with epilepsy and pneumonia as the leading treatable causes. Down syndrome was independently associated with higher odds of avoidable death (aOR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.06-1.25) and earlier age at avoidable death (aHR, 1.49; 95% CI, 1.40-1.58). Minoritized ethnic background, asthma, diabetes, and osteoporosis were each independently associated with higher odds of avoidable death, and minoritized ethnic background and greater socioeconomic deprivation with earlier age at avoidable death. Conclusions and relevance In this cohort study of adults with Down syndrome and other adults with intellectual disabilities in England, avoidable mortality exceeded that of the general population. For the adults with Down syndrome, epilepsy and pneumonia were the dominant treatable causes. These findings support proactive integrated neurological care, including epilepsy review with dementia monitoring, pneumonia prevention, and respiratory vaccination, alongside targeted interventions for minoritized ethnic groups and socioeconomically deprived groups.

item.title: Cord Serum Neonicotinoid-Related Biomarkers and Neurodevelopment From Early to Middle Childhood
item.dc:creator: Abir Nagata
Akemi Okumura
Nagahide Takahashi
Yoko Nomura
