item.description:
Authors: Abir Nagata, Akemi Okumura, Nagahide Takahashi, Yoko Nomura, Taeko Harada, Toshiki Iwabuchi, Tomoko Nishimura, Kenji J. Tsuchiya
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643481
Abstract: Importance Despite widespread neonicotinoid insecticide use, evidence on prenatal exposure and neurodevelopment beyond early childhood remains limited. Objective To examine whether cord serum concentrations of the neonicotinoid-related biomarkers dinotefuran and desmethyl-acetamiprid (dm-ACE) are associated with domain-specific neurodevelopment from infancy through middle childhood. Design, Setting, and Participants This prospective cohort study included individuals randomly selected from eligible Hamamatsu Birth Cohort for Mothers and Children Study participants born between December 2007 and March 2012 in Japan; assessments spanned ages 10 months to 9 years. Data were analyzed between October 2025 and September 2026. Exposures Cord serum dinotefuran and dm-ACE concentrations measured at birth and categorized into quartiles. Main Outcomes and Measures Outcomes were standardized scores for 5 Mullen Scales of Early Learning (MSEL) domains at ages 10 to 32 months and 4 Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (WISC-IV) indices at age 9 years. Associations were examined using linear regression and expressed as mean MSEL or WISC-IV differences in SD units at quartile 3 (Q3) and Q4 concentrations (combined Q1-Q2 was the reference). Results Among 200 individuals, 102 (51.0%) were male and 13 (6.5%) were born preterm; 185 (92.5%) to 195 (97.5%) were included in age-specific MSEL analyses and 178 (89.0%) in WISC-IV analyses. Dinotefuran groups included 96 individuals (48.0%) in Q1 and Q2, 47 (23.5%) in Q3, and 57 (28.5%) in Q4. dm-ACE groups included 82 (41.0%) in Q1 and Q2, 63 (31.5%) in Q3, and 55 (27.5%) in Q4. Early childhood associations across neurodevelopmental scale scores varied by age and concentration group, and there were no associations after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. At age 9 years, Q3 dinotefuran concentration was associated with lower WISC-IV Processing Speed Index scores compared with Q1 to Q2 scores (mean difference, −0.50 [95% CI, −0.81 to −0.20] SDs; q = .01), and Q4 dm-ACE concentration was associated with lower Perceptual Reasoning Index scores (mean difference, −0.47 [95% CI, −0.81 to −0.14] SDs; q = .03). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of infants and children in Japan, small differences in some neurodevelopmental scale scores in early childhood were observed in association with dinotefuran and dm-ACE cord serum concentrations, but there were no associations after FDR correction. At age 9 years, dinotefuran was associated with lower processing speed and dm-ACE with lower perceptual reasoning. Overall, these findings suggest domain- and age-specific associations rather than a uniform or sustained pattern across development; confirmation in larger cohorts is needed.

item.title: Bisphosphonates vs Denosumab After Low-Trauma Fractures
item.dc:creator: Mike Lin
Huy Nguyen
Thach S. Tran
Robert D. Blank
Jacqueline R. Center
Dana Bliuc
item.description:
Authors: Mike Lin, Huy Nguyen, Thach S. Tran, Robert D. Blank, Jacqueline R. Center, Dana Bliuc
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643512
Abstract: Importance Patients are at high risk of refracture and death in the immediate period following low-trauma fracture, but comparative evidence for antiresorptive therapies is limited. Objective To compare refracture and all-cause mortality between patients who initiated nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (N-BPs) and denosumab therapy after fractures. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used sequential target trial emulation of monthly trials among treatment-naive adults 50 years or older through the 12 months after incident low-trauma fracture with a new-user, active-comparator design. Linked administrative health data from the population of New South Wales, Australia, was used. Women entered from January 1, 2011, to June 30, 2018, and men from January 1, 2014, to June 30, 2018, both with 3 years of follow-up. Data were analyzed from December 1, 2025, to May 31, 2026. Exposures N-BP (alendronate, risedronate or zoledronic acid) vs denosumab. Main Outcomes and Measures Three-year all-cause mortality and refracture. Primary analyses estimated intention-to-treat (ITT) associations with inverse probability weighting. Secondary analyses included per-protocol and Fine-Gray competing-risk analyses. Hazard ratios (HRs) greater than 1.00 indicated higher risk with N-BP. Results The cohort included 15 099 participants (overall mean [SD] age, 77.2 [9.2] years), of whom 12 529 (83.0%) were women and 2570 (17.0%) were men (79.9 [8.4] years). All-cause mortality rates with N-BP vs denosumab were 48.1 vs 48.9 per 1000 person-years in women and 123.0 vs 116.4 per 1000 person-years in men, with no clear association in women (ITT HR, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87-1.10]) or men (ITT HR, 1.09 [95% CI, 0.93-1.25]). Refracture rates were 52.7 vs 46.5 per 1000 person-years in women and 70.5 vs 58.8 per 1000 person-years in men. Initiation of N-BP therapy was associated with higher refracture risk in women (ITT HR, 1.14 [95% CI, 1.05-1.26]) and men (ITT HR, 1.21 [95% CI, 1.03-1.42]). Competing-risk estimates were similar; per-protocol estimates were higher in women (HR, 1.30 [95% CI, 1.09-1.55]) and men (HR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.10-1.98]). Risks were strongest following nonhip-nonvertebral (NHNV) fractures in women (HR, 1.21 [95% CI, 1.06-1.38]) and men (HR, 1.54 [95% CI, 1.10-2.15]). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study emulating a target trial, initiation of N-BP and denosumab therapy was associated with similar mortality, whereas initiation of N-BP was associated with higher refracture risk, particularly after NHNV fractures.

item.title: Estimation of mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 COVID-19 Vaccine Effectiveness in Older US Veterans

Benjamin Skov
Frank DeVone
Amanda Wilson
Andre B. Araujo

item.description:
Authors: Kevin W. McConeghy, Benjamin Skov, Frank DeVone, Amanda Wilson, Andre B. Araujo, Nevena Vicic, Ekkehard Beck, Miao Jiang, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644727
Abstract: Importance The mRNA-1283 vaccine, a novel mRNA vaccine targeting immunodominant spike regions, was first used during the 2025-2026 respiratory virus season. Older adults remain at elevated risk for severe COVID-19 outcomes, and clinical evidence of estimated vaccine effectiveness can inform seasonal vaccination policy. Objective To compare the estimated effectiveness of mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 vaccines against medically attended COVID-19 illness and COVID-19–associated hospitalization among US veterans aged 65 years or older. Design, Setting, and Participants This was a retrospective matched cohort study emulating a target trial. US veterans aged 65 years or older who were enrolled in a national, integrated Veterans Health Administration (VHA) health care system and received an LP.8.1-formulated mRNA-1283 or BNT162b2 vaccine between August 27, 2025, and January 31, 2026, were followed up for up to 150 days or through May 1, 2026. Exposure Receipt of LP.8.1 mRNA-1283 or BNT162b2 vaccine. Main Outcome and Measures The primary outcome was medically attended COVID-19 illness, defined by a positive SARS-CoV-2 test result linked to medical care or antiviral treatment or a primary COVID-19 diagnosis. Matching was performed on home county and calendar week of vaccination, followed by inverse probability of treatment weighting. Secondary outcomes included the individual component event of hospitalization. Measures were absolute and relative differences in 150-day cumulative incidence among patients receiving mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 vaccine, computed as the estimated relative vaccine effectiveness (rVE) percentage and absolute risk difference (ARD) per 10 000 persons, adjusted for demographic and clinical factors. Results The cohort included 60 340 mRNA-1283 and 321 845 BNT162b2 vaccine recipients (mean [SD] age, 76.8 [6.7] years; 94.2% male). Among the 294 499 participants in the final matched sample, medically attended COVID-19 occurred in 86 of 55 349 mRNA-1283 vaccine recipients (0.16%) and 672 of 239 150 BNT162b2 vaccine recipients (0.28%), corresponding to estimated rVE of 35.9% (95% credible interval [CrI], 20.4%-49.7%) and an adjusted ARD of −10.0 (95% CrI, −14.3 to −5.6) events per 10 000 persons. COVID-19–associated hospitalization occurred in 11 mRNA-1283 vaccine recipients (0.02%) vs 114 BNT162b2 vaccine recipients (0.05%) (estimated rVE, 47.0% [95% CrI, 5.4%-74.8%]; adjusted ARD, −2.2 [95% CrI, −3.8 to −0.2] events per 10 000 persons). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of older US veterans during the 2025-2026 respiratory virus season, mRNA-1283 vaccination was associated with lower risks of medically attended COVID-19 outcomes and COVID-19 hospitalizations compared with BNT162b2 vaccination. The findings suggest that the mRNA-1283 vaccine may offer more clinically meaningful protection for older adults at high risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes and could inform seasonal vaccine selection.

item.title: Opioid Use and Overdose in Patients With Solid Tumor Cancers
item.dc:creator: Laura Marret
Tara Gomes
Karl Everett
Rebecca Bagnarol
Camilla Zimmermann
Jenny Lau
item.description:
Authors: Laura Marret, Tara Gomes, Karl Everett, Rebecca Bagnarol, Camilla Zimmermann, Jenny Lau
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642997
Abstract: Importance Opioids are essential for symptom control, but few studies have evaluated the association between prescription opioids and opioid overdose in oncology. Objective To describe opioid overdose in adults with solid tumor cancers and examine how opioid overdose rates vary by patient factors, cancer characteristics, and opioid prescribing. Design, Setting, and Participants This population-based, retrospective cohort study of adults in Ontario, Canada, used linked ICES data from January 1, 2013, to December 31, 2020. Participants entered the cohort at the time of newly diagnosed solid tumor cancers and were followed up from diagnosis to the first opioid overdose event, death, or December 31, 2024. Data analysis was performed from August to December 2025. Exposure Exposure was outpatient opioid prescription dose and duration reassessed every 30 days. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was a fatal or the first nonfatal opioid overdose event. Results Among 554 316 adults with cancer (mean [SD] age, 63.8 [16.2], 57.1 [17.2], and 45.8 [13.7] years for the no, nonfatal, and fatal opioid overdose groups, respectively; 308 903 [55.9%], 921 [59.5%], and 116 [60.7%] female for the no, nonfatal, and fatal opioid overdose groups, respectively), 1591 (0.3%) had 1 or more nonfatal opioid overdoses, and 191 (0.03%) had a fatal opioid overdose. In the first year after diagnosis, patients with stage III and IV cancers had substantially higher rates of any opioid overdose than those with stage I (stage III vs I: hazard ratio [HR], 2.55; 95% CI, 1.96-3.31; stage IV vs I: HR, 6.24; 95% CI, 4.68-8.31). After adjustment, any opioid prescription in the prior 30 days was associated with 71% higher combined nonfatal and fatal opioid overdose rate (HR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.47-2.00), and approximately 3.5 times higher if prescribed high-dose opioids (≥50-mg morphine-equivalent daily dose; HR, 3.47; 95% CI, 2.97-4.05). Recently prescribed opioids were associated with increased opioid overdose risk in patients with cancer without opioid use disorder (any dose: HR, 1.80; 95% CI, 1.54-2.11; high dose: HR, 3.76; 95% CI, 3.21-4.41). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of adults with solid tumor cancers, opioid overdose was rare and highest in the first year after diagnosis and in patients with advanced cancer; opioid overdose risk increased with every month high-dose opioids were prescribed. The findings suggest that opioids should be prescribed at the lowest effective dose for symptom management, with close monitoring and routine assessment for opioid overdose risk.

item.title: Social Determinants of Health and Long-Term, Device-Based Sleep Health
item.dc:creator: Esha Narla
Fang Zhu
May A. Beydoun
Dayna A. Johnson
Tené T. Lewis
Daniel J. Gottlieb
Tianyi Huang
item.description:
Authors: Esha Narla, Fang Zhu, May A. Beydoun, Dayna A. Johnson, Tené T. Lewis, Daniel J. Gottlieb, Tianyi Huang
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643802
Abstract: Importance Prior research on social determinants of health (SDOH) and sleep health has largely relied on subjective sleep measures, primarily self-reported sleep duration. Evidence remains limited on the associations between SDOH and wearable-derived long-term sleep patterns in large-scale populations. Objective To examine how SDOH (overall and by domain) are associated with long-term, wearable-derived sleep duration and variability. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study included participants from the All of Us Research Program enrolled between 2018 and 2023 who contributed at least 180 days of wearable data, including pre-enrollment historical records, and completed the SDOH survey. Data analysis was conducted from September 2025 to June 2026. Exposures Measures of overall and domain-specific SDOH, including social and community context, economic stability, neighborhood environment, and health care access and quality, were derived from validated surveys and standardized to z scores. Main Outcomes and Measures Mean daily sleep duration (in minutes) and day-to-day sleep duration SD across all available days were calculated from device-estimated main sleep episodes. Results Among 12 403 participants (mean [SD] age, 57.8 [15.2] years; 8719 female [70.3%]; 10 946 White [88.3%] and 1457 members of minority racial groups [11.7%]; 756 Hispanic [6.1%]), 9052 individuals (73.0%) had a college degree or above, with a mean (SD) sleep duration of 406.1 (44.9) minutes and a mean (SD) sleep duration SD of 76.9 (20.6) minutes. Participants were monitored for a median (range) of 982 (180 to 4133) days. Compared with participants in the lowest SDOH tertile, those in the highest tertile (indicating more favorable social and structural conditions) had 5.82 minutes (95% CI, 3.84 to 7.80 minutes) longer sleep duration and 4.79 minutes (95% CI, −5.69 to −3.89 minutes) lower sleep duration SD in the fully adjusted model. When examining individual SDOH domains, economic stability showed the strongest associations with mean sleep duration (eg, 10.70 minutes; 95% CI, 5.30 to 16.10 minutes) and sleep duration SD (eg, −8.70 minutes; 95% CI, −11.20 to −6.26 minutes). Limited subgroup heterogeneity in the association was observed across age, sex, race, and ethnicity. Conclusions and Relevance In this study, more favorable SDOH conditions were associated with longer and more regular habitual sleep duration over the long term, emphasizing the importance of social and structural factors when evaluating sleep health.

item.title: Ibuprofen Use and Acute Kidney Injury Among Adults Admitted to the Hospital
item.dc:creator: Haedi E. Thelen
Luke J. Keele
Christina Brotman
Michael G.S. Shashaty
Todd A. Miano
item.description:
Authors: Haedi E. Thelen, Luke J. Keele, Christina Brotman, Michael G.S. Shashaty, Todd A. Miano
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642745
Abstract: Importance Although nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the most effective nonopioid analgesics for acute pain, they may be underused in the inpatient setting due to uncertainty regarding the risk of acute kidney injury (AKI). Whether inpatient exposure to NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, substantially increases AKI risk and how ibuprofen-associated AKI varies across patient subgroups remain unknown. Objective To determine whether ibuprofen use is associated with AKI in hospitalized patients and whether the finding varies across AKI risk factor subgroups. Design, Setting, and Participants A retrospective active-comparator cohort study of hospitalized patients (aged ≥18 years) without end-stage kidney disease or contraindications to NSAID treatment admitted from January 1, 2004, to June 30, 2017, in a large academic health system including 3 hospitals in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, with follow-up until 48 hours after treatment end, hospital discharge, or 14 days elapsed, whichever occurred first. Analyses were conducted from March 2023 through August 2026. Exposures At least 24 hours of treatment with ibuprofen or oxycodone for acute pain. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was AKI, defined by changes in serum creatinine and incident kidney replacement therapy (KRT). Balancing weights were used to adjust for baseline covariates and weighted Poisson regression used to estimate incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and 95% CIs. Results This study included 78 656 patients (median age, 59 [IQR, 47-69] years; 38 092 females [48%]) treated with ibuprofen (n = 6313) or oxycodone (n = 72 343). There were 4799 AKI events (79% stage 1) during 270 472 days of follow-up (17.7 events per 1000 days). After adjustment for baseline differences, patients treated with ibuprofen had a higher rate of any AKI (IRR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.09-1.38), severe AKI (IRR, 1.36; 95% CI, 1.08-1.72), and KRT (IRR, 3.29; 95% CI, 1.35-8.03). IRRs were greater in postoperative (IRR, 1.70 [95% CI, 1.28-2.27] vs 1.12 [95% CI, 0.98-1.28]) and critically ill (IRR, 1.65 [95% CI, 1.29-2.11] vs 1.16 [95% CI, 1.02-1.33]) patients. In patients at low risk (those non–critically ill, nonpostoperative, aged &amp;lt;60 years without kidney dysfunction; ibuprofen, n = 2966; oxycodone, n = 20 440), ibuprofen was not associated with higher AKI risk (IRR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.75-1.18). Conclusions and Relevance This study in an inpatient cohort found that ibuprofen was associated with higher rates of AKI and KRT, but this excess risk was concentrated in patients at high risk. Patients at low risk may be able to receive ibuprofen safely yet were often prescribed oxycodone.

item.title: Chemotherapy-Induced Biological Age Acceleration and Lifetime Outcomes in Breast Cancer Survivors
item.dc:creator: Swarnavo Sarkar
Mina S. Sedrak
Judith E. Carroll
Clyde Schechter
Hyman B. Muss
Jeanne S. Mandelblatt
item.description:
Authors: Swarnavo Sarkar, Mina S. Sedrak, Judith E. Carroll, Clyde Schechter, Hyman B. Muss, Jeanne S. Mandelblatt
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643008
Abstract: Importance Growing evidence suggests some breast cancer survivors may experience accelerated aging (biological age in excess of chronological age) after receiving chemotherapy. Objective To quantify the range of lifetime changes in accelerated aging following chemotherapy. Design, Setting, and Participants This comparative effectiveness study used an established Cancer Intervention and Surveillance Modeling Network breast cancer model integrating biological aging with breast cancer epidemiology. Biological aging was modeled using data on distributions of postchemotherapy senescence measured by p16 INK4a levels, and the model assumed chemotherapy-induced senescence only affected non–breast cancer mortality. The simulated population included US women diagnosed with breast cancer at ages 30 to 79 years between 1990 and 2030, with follow-up until death. Two model simulations were run; the first assumed all women who developed breast cancer received anthracycline, and the second assumed all received nonanthracycline treatment. Modeling was conducted from November 2025 to April 2026. Results were validated by comparing model-predicted trends with findings from the Anthracycline for Early Breast Cancer (ABC) trials. Exposures More vs less cytotoxic chemotherapy, using exemplar anthracycline-based vs nonanthracycline regimens. Main Outcomes and Measures Lifetime outcomes included the age at which the risk of non–breast cancer mortality exceeded the risk of breast cancer mortality by chemotherapy regimen, posttreatment life-years, and all-cause mortality by age group at diagnosis and median senescence levels. Results The study included a simulated population of 400 million US women aged 30 to 79 years diagnosed with breast cancer. Breast cancer survivors who received anthracycline lost 9.4 (IQR, 7.6-11.2) years of remaining life years. Overall, among anthracycline recipients, the risk of non–breast cancer mortality was projected to exceed breast cancer mortality 16 (IQR, 12-19) years earlier than expected based on chronological age. There was heterogeneity in results, with greater variability for women diagnosed at younger vs older ages. Women receiving more vs less cytotoxic regimens were estimated to lose a median difference of 7.6 (IQR, 7.0-8.0) more years of life due to earlier ages at onset of aging-related diseases. The model closely replicated all-cause and 8-year breast cancer survival trends in the ABC trials. Conclusions and Relevance In this simulation model of chemotherapy-induced biological aging, increased breast cancer survival was seen with more (vs less) cytotoxic regimens, but this was paired with greater potential risk of earlier non–breast cancer mortality due to age acceleration. These results suggest the value of integrating knowledge about biological aging into survivorship care and could inform future research to address accelerated aging among breast cancer survivors.

item.title: Inhaled Corticosteroids and Sickle Cell Disease Severity in Adults Without Asthma
item.dc:creator: Susanna A. Curtis
Sarah McCuskee
Robyn T. Cohen
Angela Liu
Marc A. Probst
Tiffany Mitchell
Jordan Bellis
Bin Zhang
item.description:
Authors: Susanna A. Curtis, Sarah McCuskee, Robyn T. Cohen, Angela Liu, Marc A. Probst, Tiffany Mitchell, Jordan Bellis, Bin Zhang, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642232
Abstract: Importance People living with sickle cell disease (SCD) who have episodic cough and wheeze (ECW) without a diagnosis of asthma have high rates of pain episodes and acute chest syndrome. A previous trial, in which patients with SCD and ECW without asthma received 15 weeks of inhaled mometasone or placebo, showed that inhaled mometasone improved daily pain and reduced soluble vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1), a marker of disease severity in SCD. Objective To examine the biologic effects and safety of long-term daily inhaled mometasone in patients without asthma but with SCD and ECW. Design, Setting, and Participants This placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial recruited patients with SCD from December 2018 to May 2022. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either inhaled mometasone or placebo for 48 weeks. Data analyses followed the modified intention-to-treat principle and were performed between July and November 2023. Interventions The inhaled mometasone group received 220 μg of inhaled mometasone furoate dry powder once daily. The placebo group received a matching placebo inhaler. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was percentage change in soluble VCAM-1 levels from baseline to end of study. Secondary outcomes included laboratory results, functional outcomes, patient-reported outcomes, and health care utilization. Results Of the 77 patients who received the intervention and were included in the analysis, 40 were assigned to inhaled mometasone (mean [SD] age, 36.0 [11.6] years; 26 females [65%]) and 37 were assigned to placebo (mean [SD] age, 31.5 [8.6] years; 19 males [51%]). Compared with the placebo group, the inhaled mometasone group increased their soluble VCAM-1 levels by 42% (95% CI, –11% to 96%; P = .02). Point estimates for clinical outcomes favored the placebo group, although the findings were not statistically significant. Conclusions and Relevance In this trial of adults with SCD and ECW, extended courses of inhaled mometasone were associated with worsened markers of disease severity. Inhaled mometasone should not be used long-term in patients with SCD and ECW without a definitive diagnosis of asthma. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03758950

item.title: Automated Clinical Decision Support and Electronic Health Record Tracking of Patients With Adenomas Found on Colonoscopy
item.dc:creator: Michael T. O’Brien
Ashley Spann
Laura Zahn
Allison McCoy
Sara N. Horst
item.description:
Authors: Michael T. O’Brien, Ashley Spann, Laura Zahn, Allison McCoy, Sara N. Horst
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641560
Abstract: Importance Surveillance colonoscopy following adenoma detection is essential for colorectal cancer prevention, yet systematic tracking within electronic health record (EHR) systems remains challenging, as they rely on manual data entry. Objective To determine if implementation of an automatic tool in the EHR is associated with improved health care maintenance table updates for patients needing repeat colonoscopy for cancer screening after adenoma detection. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study at a single tertiary care center within a large health care organization with EHR functionality included patients undergoing colonoscopy between November 2017 and December 2024. Eligible participants were adults aged 50 to 75 years undergoing colonoscopy for screening, surveillance, or diagnostic indications. Exclusion criteria included patients with inflammatory bowel disease, known colorectal cancer, or hereditary cancer syndromes. Data were analyzed between January and May 2025. Exposure A decision support tool was implemented that allowed gastroenterologists completing colonoscopies for patients with adenoma to choose follow-up intervals that would automatically populate the health maintenance tab. Main Outcomes and Measures Rate of updates of the health maintenance table and percentage completion from gastroenterology vs primary care. Results A total of 35 802 patients met criteria (20 049 female [56.0%]; median [range] age: preintervention, 61 years [50-75 years]; postintervention, 62 years [50-75 years]); adenomas were detected in 8004 of 18 027 patients (44.4%) in the preintervention period and 8396 of 17 775 patients (47.2%) in the postintervention period. Health maintenance updates for patients with adenomas requiring closer surveillance increased significantly, from 83.4% (6672 of 8004 patients) to 94.2% (7913 of 8396 patients) following the intervention ( P &amp;lt; .001). Gastroenterology team completion of health maintenance updates increased postintervention from 67.6% (5413 of 8004 patients) to 91.9% (7717 of 8396 patients). Conversely, primary care team updates decreased significantly from 9.3% (746 of 8004 patients) to 1.4% (118 of 8396 patients) following the intervention ( P &amp;lt; .001 for both). Population health automatic updates occurred in a small number of patients in both periods. Conclusions and Relevance Implementation of automatic updates to the health maintenance section of the EHR was associated with significantly increased the reliability of postadenoma surveillance documentation; after the intervention, gastroenterology reporting increased while the primary care burden was reduced. These findings suggest that clinical decision support implementation is critical for accurate adenoma surveillance intervals.

item.dc:creator: Leon Z. Jia
Narek Israelyan
Frances S. Shofer
Sameh Saleh
Jeffrey Moon
Mika Epps
Joy Iocca
Sean Foster
item.description:
Authors: Leon Z. Jia, Narek Israelyan, Frances S. Shofer, Sameh Saleh, Jeffrey Moon, Mika Epps, Joy Iocca, Sean Foster, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642980
Abstract: Importance High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) assays are the diagnostic standard for acute coronary syndrome but present significant implementation and workflow complexity. Objective To evaluate whether implementation of a structured, electronic health record (EHR)–integrated hs-cTn pathway was associated with changes in emergency department (ED) length of stay (LOS) and serial troponin testing times. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective quality improvement study compared preimplementation conventional cTn assay (June 1, 2021, to March 31, 2022) with a postimplementation integrated hs-cTn pathway (June 1, 2022, to March 31, 2023) in 4 urban EDs within a single health system. Participants were adults (aged ≥18 years) presenting with chest pain and at least 1 troponin assay result. Data analysis was performed from April to September 2024. Exposures Implementation of an hs-cTn assay within an EHR-integrated clinical pathway. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was ED LOS, defined as time from patient registration to ED departure. Secondary outcomes included time from first clinician evaluation to disposition (discharge or admission) and interval from the first troponin assay order to the second troponin assay result in patients with serial assays. Results Of the 16 094 patient encounters analyzed (9151 [56.9%] female; mean [SD] age, 49.5 [17.4] years), 8486 (52.7%) were in the hs-cTn and 7608 (47.3%) were in the conventional cTn cohort. Overall, hs-cTn implementation with workflow integration was associated with decreased mean ED LOS, from 6.18 (95% CI, 6.10-6.26) hours to 5.64 (95% CI, 5.57-5.71) hours. Compared with conventional cTn, implementation of the hs-cTn pathway was associated with shorter mean ED LOS in admitted patients (9.60 [95% CI, 9.35-9.87] hours vs 10.50 [95% CI, 10.22-10.78] hours; P = .003) and discharged patients (5.02 [95% CI, 4.96-5.08] hours vs 5.33 [95% CI, 5.26-5.40] hours; P = .006). Pathway implementation was also associated with shorter time from evaluation to disposition in patients receiving 2 or more troponin measurements (5.06 [95% CI, 4.97-5.15] hours vs 6.68 [95% CI, 6.52-6.85] hours; P &amp;lt; .001) and time from first troponin order to second troponin result in both admitted patients (3.18 [95% CI, 3.11-3.25] hours vs 5.16 [95% CI, 5.01-5.31] hours; P &amp;lt; .001) and discharged patients (2.78 [95% CI, 2.75-2.82] hours vs 4.54 [95% CI, 4.46-4.62] hours; P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this quality improvement study, an EHR-integrated hs-cTn pathway was associated with significantly reduced ED LOS and, in patients with serial troponin measurements, reduced time from evaluation to disposition and reduced time to serial assay results. The findings suggest this structured EHR approach may mitigate operational challenges of hs-cTn adoption and could serve as a scalable model to improve ED efficiency for patients with chest pain.

item.title: Differences in Health and Access to Care Between Heterosexual and Sexual Minority Health Care Professionals
item.dc:creator: Gilbert Gonzales
Eric Connelly
Christopher Terndrup
Jesse M. Ehrenfeld
item.description:
Authors: Gilbert Gonzales, Eric Connelly, Christopher Terndrup, Jesse M. Ehrenfeld
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643017
Abstract: Importance Little is known about the health and access to care of sexual minority health care professionals (HCPs). Objective To compare health outcomes, health insurance coverage, and access to care between sexual minority and heterosexual HCPs. Design, Setting, and Participants For this survey study, cross-sectional data analysis of the 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024 National Health Interview Surveys was performed. The study population included nationally representative household probability samples of noninstitutionalized US civilian adults aged 18 years or older, restricted to HCPs working in health care settings. Data analysis was conducted between February 2024 and August 2026. Exposure Self-reported sexual orientation, categorized as sexual minority (gay, lesbian, bisexual, or another nonheterosexual identity) or heterosexual. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcomes included cigarette smoking, lifetime diagnosis of depression, moderate to severe psychological distress, selected physical health conditions, primary source of health insurance coverage, and delayed or forgone medical care, mental health care, and prescription medications due to cost. Multivariable logistic regression models compared outcomes while adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Results The sample included 2890 HCPs (2731 heterosexual and 159 sexual minority; mean [SE] age, 44.9 [0.7] years; 74.7% [0.9%] female [survey weighted]). Sexual minority individuals represented 5.7% (95% CI, 4.8%-6.7%) of HCPs and were more likely to be younger (aged 26-34 years: 38.8% [95% CI, 30.1%-48.3%] vs 24.0% [95% CI, 22.2%-25.9%]), never married (32.7% [95% CI, 24.7%-41.8%] vs 14.6% [95% CI, 13.0%-16.4%]), and living in households below the federal poverty level (7.4% [95% CI, 3.4%-15.4%] vs 1.1% [95% CI, 0.7%-1.7%]) compared with heterosexual HCPs. Sexual minority HCPs were significantly more likely to report a lifetime diagnosis of depression (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 3.05 [95% CI, 2.02-4.59]), moderate to severe psychological distress (AOR, 2.06 [95% CI, 1.23-3.46]), arthritis (AOR, 2.45 [95% CI, 1.42-4.22]), and delayed medical care due to cost (AOR, 2.06 [95% CI, 1.14-3.72]). Sexual minority HCPs faced greater disparities in access to care: they were more likely to forgo mental health care (AOR, 3.74 [95% CI, 2.11-6.63]) and to forgo prescription medications (AOR, 4.81 [95% CI, 2.52-9.15]) due to cost than their heterosexual peers. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional survey study of HCPs, sexual minority HCPs were more likely than heterosexual HCPs to report depression, psychological distress, and financial barriers to health care. These findings highlight disparities in health and access to care among sexual minority HCPs and the need for workplace supports to address factors contributing to these disparities.

item.title: Inforatio Technique and Foot Ulcer Closure Among Patients With Diabetes
item.dc:creator: Sahar Moeini
Hans Gottlieb
Tue Smith Jørgensen
Malene Ringholm Bæk Larsen
Stig Brorson
item.description:
Authors: Sahar Moeini, Hans Gottlieb, Tue Smith Jørgensen, Malene Ringholm Bæk Larsen, Stig Brorson
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642733
Abstract: Importance Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are common complications of diabetes, a disease increasing in prevalence worldwide. Novel adjunctive treatments that are affordable and feasible to implement in both high- and low-income settings are urgently needed. Objective To assess whether the inforatio technique promotes healing of DFUs compared with standard of care (SOC). Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter, evaluator-blinded randomized clinical trial was conducted at 4 outpatient clinics specializing in wound care in Denmark from February 15, 2022, to December 18, 2024. One-year medical record follow-up was completed August 14, 2025. Participants included patients with noninfected Wagner grade 1 DFUs. Interventions Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive the inforatio technique every third week for 12 weeks with SOC or SOC only. The inforatio technique involved making incisions on wound beds with 2-mm biopsy punch tools. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the proportion of ulcers achieving closure within 20 weeks. Secondary outcomes were health-related and disease-specific quality of life. Safety outcomes included serious and target ulcer–related adverse events. Results A total of 101 patients were randomized, of whom 100 had DFUs and were included in the primary analysis (49 in the inforatio group and 51 in the SOC only group; 85 men; mean [SD] age, 64.4 [11.4] years; median ulcer size, 0.76 [range, 0.09-23.23] cm 2 ). Twenty-four patients in the inforatio group (49.0%) vs 14 in the SOC-only group (27.5%) achieved ulcer closure within 20 weeks (adjusted odds ratio, 3.01 [95% CI, 1.20-7.58]; P = .02). No between-group difference was found in quality of life change from baseline to 20 weeks. Within 20 weeks, 7 patients in the inforatio group vs 13 in the SOC-only group experienced the serious adverse events, including death, amputation, or target ulcer–related hospitalization (relative risk, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.24-1.29]; P = .25), and 16 patients in the inforatio group vs 30 in the SOC-only group experienced target ulcer–related adverse events (relative risk, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.35-0.88]; P = .02). Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial, the inforatio technique improved DFU healing compared with SOC alone. Fewer ulcer-related adverse events were also observed with the inforatio technique, although this exploratory finding should be interpreted cautiously. Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642912
Abstract: Importance Neighborhood social disadvantage (NSD) is increasingly recognized as being associated with health disparities. However, its associations with longitudinal lung function decline, health-related quality of life (HRQOL), and mortality remain incompletely understood. Objective To evaluate associations of NSD with lung function, HRQOL, and all-cause mortality and to explore potential mediators of any association. Design, Setting, and Participants Prospective cohort study of current and former smokers aged 40 to 75 years with at least 10 pack-years of smoking history in the Lovelace Smokers Cohort. Participants underwent repeated spirometry approximately every 18 months from 2001 through 2017. Mortality was ascertained through October 2020 using the National Death Index. Data were analyzed from January to May 2025. Exposures Census tract–level Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and Social Deprivation Index (SDI) assigned to residential addresses. Main Outcomes and Measures Baseline and longitudinal lung function (forced expiratory volume in 1 second [FEV1], forced vital capacity [FVC], and the FEV1:FVC ratio), baseline HRQOL assessed by the St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ), with higher scores indicating poorer respiratory health status, and the 36-item Short Form Survey, and all-cause mortality. Formal mediation analyses evaluated educational attainment, current smoking status, and dietary patterns, whereas baseline lung function and HRQOL were considered as potential mediators for associations of NSD with all-cause mortality. Results Among 2362 included participants, the mean (SD) baseline age was 56.3 (9.4) years, and 1738 (73.58%) were female. A 1-IQR increase in SDI was associated with lower baseline FEV1 (β, −0.09 [95% CI, −0.13 to −0.06] L) and FEV1:FVC ratio (β, −1.21 [95% CI, −1.80 to −0.62] percentage points). Higher SVI was associated with faster annual decline in FEV1 (β, −3.11 [95% CI, −5.86 to −0.36] mL/y) and FEV1:FVC ratio (β, −0.05 [95% CI, −0.11 to −0.001] percentage points/y), worse baseline HRQOL, including a higher SGRQ total score (β, 4.46 [95% CI, 3.26-5.65] points), and higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.08-1.53]). Current smoking status and 2 dietary pattern scores mediated 4.4% (95% CI, −1.2% to 12.8%) to 31.0% (95% CI, 13.0%-51.6%) and 4.5% (95% CI, 0.2%-12.9%) to 17.0% (95% CI, 5.5%-113.7%), respectively, of selected associations between NSD and lung health outcomes; baseline lung function and HRQOL mediated 6.7% (95% CI, 0.6%-22.8%) to 38.6% (95% CI, 19.9%-125.3%) of selected associations with all-cause mortality. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, worse NSD was associated with faster lung function decline, worse HRQOL, and higher all-cause mortality among ever smokers. Mediation analyses suggested that current smoking status and dietary patterns may partially account for associations of NSD with lung function and HRQOL.

item.title: Perioperative Antibiotic Use in Head and Neck Surgery
item.dc:creator: Markus Blaurock
Petr Szturz
Simon Andreas Mueller
Michael Knoke
Nadine Höpfner
Nils-Olaf Hübner
Johanna Inhestern
Elena Colombo
item.description:
Authors: Markus Blaurock, Petr Szturz, Simon Andreas Mueller, Michael Knoke, Nadine Höpfner, Nils-Olaf Hübner, Johanna Inhestern, Elena Colombo, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642922
Abstract: Importance Perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis in head and neck surgery remains poorly standardized internationally, despite evidence supporting short-course regimens and showing no benefit in low-risk procedures. Contemporary international data on prescribing practice are limited. Objectives To characterize international patterns of perioperative antibiotic use in endocrine and oncologic head and neck surgery and to identify discrepancies between reported practice and evidence-based recommendations. Design, Setting, and Participants In this survey study, a cross-sectional survey was distributed electronically between October 1, 2024, and December 31, 2025, through national and international professional societies. Respondents were classified by country of practice into Europe, North America, and rest of world. Data were analyzed in June 2026. Main Outcomes and Measures Routine antibiotic use, agent selection, and duration of prophylaxis across 6 procedure categories (conventional thyroidectomy, completion thyroidectomy, complex thyroidectomy, low-risk head and neck squamous cell carcinoma [HNSCC], low-complexity HNSCC, and complex clean-contaminated HNSCC). Secondary outcomes were departmental guideline availability and circumstances prompting antibiotic use. Results Of 468 respondents (310 of 419 [74%] with available data reported male sex or gender, 32 of 432 [82%] otolaryngologists–head and neck surgeons and 283 of 431 [66%] in academic practice), routine antibiotic use for conventional thyroidectomy was reported by 12% (95% CI, 8%-19%) of European, 35% (95% CI, 27%-44%) of North American, and 56% (95% CI, 39%-71%) of rest of world respondents. For clean-contaminated HNSCC, prophylaxis use ranged from 93% to 99%, with aminopenicillin plus a β-lactamase inhibitor preferred in Europe (66%) and North America (64%); cefazolin predominated in North America (47%) and cefuroxime in Europe (31%). For low-complexity clean-contaminated procedures, 24-hour regimens were reported by 43% (95% CI, 34%–53%) of North American vs 11% (95% CI, 7%–16%) of European respondents, whereas 7-day courses were reported by 23% (95% CI, 17%–29%) of European vs 8% (95% CI, 4%–15%) of North American respondents. Departmental HNSCC guidelines were more available in Europe than North America (83% vs 38%). Conclusions and Relevance In this survey study of 468 head and neck surgeons, perioperative antibiotic prescribing was heterogeneous internationally, with routine use in clean procedures and prolonged regimens for clean-contaminated surgery. Departmental guideline availability did not correspond to shorter reported prophylaxis duration, suggesting that implementation rather than guideline existence may be the target for antimicrobial stewardship.

item.title: Drug Therapies and Incidence of Dementia Among Adults With Overactive Bladder
item.dc:creator: David Sheyn
Stephen Rhodes
Zeinab Mohamed
Adonis Hijaz
item.description:
Authors: David Sheyn, Stephen Rhodes, Zeinab Mohamed, Adonis Hijaz
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642026
Abstract: Importance Concern that anticholinergic medications for overactive bladder (OAB) are associated with increased dementia risk has encouraged a shift toward β3 adrenergic agonists, which are presumed cognitively safer. Whether this presumption is justified is uncertain. Objective To compare the risk of incident dementia among adults initiating high-risk anticholinergic, low-risk anticholinergic, or β3 agonist therapy for OAB and to evaluate the association of treatment duration with risk. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used Epic Cosmos electronic health record data from 2012 to 2025. Adults aged 40 to 90 years newly treated for OAB within 1 year of diagnosis without preexisting dementia were included. Exposures First prescribed medication class: high-risk anticholinergics (oxybutynin, tolterodine, or solifenacin), low-risk anticholinergics (darifenacin, trospium, or fesoterodine), or β3 agonists (mirabegron or vibegron). Main Outcomes and Measures Incident dementia by diagnosis code or dementia-specific medication. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and Cox proportional hazards models were used, with analyses stratified by age and sex and an exploratory landmark duration-response analysis. Results Among 830 393 patients (585 198 female [70.5%]; median [IQR] age, 67 [57-76] years), incident dementia occurred in 65 134 patients, with a median (IQR) follow-up ranging from 1046 (571-1809) days for β3 agonists to 1568 (857-2614) days for high-risk anticholinergics. After IPTW, high-risk anticholinergics were associated with a lower hazard of dementia than β3 agonists (hazard ratio [HR], 0.90; 95% CI, 0.87-0.93) and low-risk anticholinergics (HR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.96); low-risk anticholinergics did not differ from β3 agonists (HR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.93-1.01). Weighted 10-year dementia risk was highest for β3 agonists (20.0%; 95% CI, 18.8%-21.2%) and lowest for high-risk anticholinergics (18.1%; 95% CI, 17.9%-18.3%). E-values of 1.29 (high-risk anticholinergics vs β3 agonists) and 1.20 (high-risk vs low-risk anticholinergics) suggested that observed differences could be explained by a modest amount of unmeasured confounding. Longer anticholinergic duration was not associated with increased risk. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of patients undergoing treatment for OAB, β3 agonists were not associated with a lower dementia incidence compared with anticholinergics. These findings suggest that previously reported increases in risk may reflect residual confounding rather than a pharmacological effect.

item.title: A Scalable Teacher Professional Development and Wellness Program in Primary Schools
item.dc:creator: Keng-Yen Huang
Janet Nakigudde
Hyung G. Park
Eddie Tinka Mugisa
Christine Tusiime
Elizabeth Nsamba Kisakye
Sabrina Cheng
Michelle Boyd
item.description:
Authors: Keng-Yen Huang, Janet Nakigudde, Hyung G. Park, Eddie Tinka Mugisa, Christine Tusiime, Elizabeth Nsamba Kisakye, Sabrina Cheng, Michelle Boyd, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642259
Abstract: Importance In Uganda and other low-income settings with prevalent mental health problems and limited resources, scalable professional development (PD) models are needed to strengthen teachers’ capacity to apply evidence-based practices to support child mental health. Objective To examine the short-term effectiveness of PD and PD with a teacher-wellness enhancement (PDT) compared with a control condition on teacher knowledge and use of evidence-based practices, teacher stress, and teacher stress management; implementation outcomes; and the differential outcomes between urban and rural primary schools in Uganda. Design, Setting, and Participants This cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 47 urban and rural schools in Uganda between August 2021 and February 2025. Participating teachers in the schools were followed-up 24 months after the intervention, and the present trial focused on short-term teacher outcomes. Statistical analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle. Interventions Schools and teachers were randomized to 1 of 3 conditions: PD, PDT, and control. The PD intervention (mWEL-PD or Mental Wellbeing and Empowering Lives of the School Community: Professional Development) consisted of 3 days of training and 8 one-hour coaching sessions in person for 2 to 3 months. The PDT intervention (mWEL-PD with a teacher-wellness enhancement) was provided as the PD program plus a 1-day workshop and 3 group support sessions. The control condition offered no intervention during year 1, but mental health knowledge and promotion materials and a 1-day teacher-wellness workshop were provided in year 2. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcomes for PD and PDT groups were knowledge and use of evidence-based practices. Teachers completed 15 self-report measures assessing 4 key outcomes: knowledge of evidence-based practices, use of evidence-based practices, teacher stress, and teacher stress management. Implementation outcomes, self-assessed after completion of the intervention, included teacher engagement in the intervention, teacher perception of acceptability and usefulness of the content, and teacher perception of the competence of the program facilitators. Results A total of 47 schools with 509 teachers (mean [SD] age, 40.60 [11.12] years; 368 females [72.3%]) were included in the analysis. Among the schools, 15 (31.9%) were randomly assigned to the control, 16 (34.0%) to the PD, and 16 (34.0%) to the PDT groups. Among teachers, 165 (32.4%) were randomly assigned to the control, 187 (36.7%) to the PD, and 157 (30.8%) to the PDT groups. Teacher attendance at training and coaching sessions and ratings of relevance and facilitator competence were high in both urban and rural contexts. Compared with teachers in the PD group, those in the PDT group were more likely to attend all training days offered (120 of 187 [64.1%] in the PD group vs 127 of 157 [80.9%] in the PDT group) and participated in more coaching sessions (mean [SD] number, 4.58 [2.91] vs 6.09 [2.28]). Compared with teachers in the control condition, teachers in the PDT condition benefited on all 4 key outcomes: increased knowledge (standardized mean difference [SMD], 0.57; 95% CI, 0.26-0.88) and use (SMD, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.01-0.71) of evidence-based practices, increased stress management (SMD, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.19-0.80), and decreased stress (SMD, −0.27; 95% CI, −0.54 to 0.01). Benefits of PD were limited to knowledge of evidence-based practices (SMD, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.03-0.62). Conclusions and Relevance This trial of a scalable teacher PD program delivered through existing educational infrastructure and resources demonstrates the program’s feasibility, acceptability, and impact on self-reported teacher outcomes. The finding of short-term benefits for teacher practice and wellness suggests the potential of the PDT model for school-based mental health promotion. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04383327

item.title: Primary Endocrine Therapy vs Upfront Surgery for Older Women With Estrogen Receptor–Positive Breast Cancer
item.dc:creator: Neil Carleton
Jian Zou
Yangyang Mu
Steffi Oesterreich
Shannon Puhalla
Julia Foldi
George Tseng
Adrian V. Lee
item.description:
Authors: Neil Carleton, Jian Zou, Yangyang Mu, Steffi Oesterreich, Shannon Puhalla, Julia Foldi, George Tseng, Adrian V. Lee, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643218
Abstract: Importance As the population of older women with breast cancer grows, an increasing number are considered for primary endocrine therapy (pET), yet clinicians lack a framework for identifying which patients are appropriate candidates, resulting in reliance on chronologic age and life expectancy rather than tumor biology. Objective To evaluate survival and variables associated with response duration for patients treated with pET. Data Sources PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception through March 26, 2026. Study Selection Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and non-RCT (observational) cohorts comparing pET with surgery in operable, nonmetastatic, estrogen receptor (ER)–positive breast cancer. Data Extraction and Synthesis Data were extracted independently by 2 reviewers per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Hazard ratios (HRs) not directly reported were reconstructed from Kaplan-Meier curves. Randomized clinical trial–derived HRs for overall survival (OS) and breast cancer–specific survival (BCSS) were pooled using a random-effects model, given anticipated heterogeneity across trials spanning 5 decades and differing tumor biology criteria. Observational cohorts were analyzed descriptively, not pooled for comparative survival, given susceptibility to confounding by indication. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcomes were OS and BCSS (RCTs) assessed using meta-analysis. Time to progression, salvage intervention rates, and variables associated with progression and mortality (observational cohorts) were assessed using descriptive analyses. Results Twenty-nine studies (6 RCTs and 23 observational cohorts; 22 821 patients; overall median [IQR] age, 83.1 [77.0-85.0] years) met the inclusion criteria. Patients from RCTs were generally younger (median [IQR] age, 77.0 [75.8-78.0] years) than those from the observational studies (median [IQR] age, 84.0 [81.5-86.0] years). Treatment with pET was not associated with a statistically significant OS difference vs surgery (HR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.98-1.33), though the point estimate favored surgery. Median time to progression ranged from 19.7 months (range, 13.5-26.0 months) in tumor biology–unselected, tamoxifen-era cohorts to more than 50 months in ER-selected and aromatase inhibitor–treated cohorts. Tumor biology was consistently associated with progression risk. Conclusions and Relevance This systematic review and meta-analysis of more than 22 000 patients with ER-positive breast cancer found no statistically significant survival difference between pET and upfront surgery. Durable disease control under pET seemed to be concentrated in patients with favorable biology. These findings support a framework incorporating tumor biology and frailty, rather than age alone, to identify candidates for pET.

item.title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Mammography Outcomes by Advanced Breast Cancer Risk
item.dc:creator: Karla Kerlikowske
Linn Abraham
Weiwei Zhu
Brian L. Sprague
Anna N. A. Tosteson
Erin J. Aiello Bowles
Christoph I. Lee
Diana L. Miglioretti
item.description:
Authors: Karla Kerlikowske, Linn Abraham, Weiwei Zhu, Brian L. Sprague, Anna N. A. Tosteson, Erin J. Aiello Bowles, Christoph I. Lee, Diana L. Miglioretti
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642398
Abstract: Importance Few studies have examined advanced breast cancer rates in women undergoing routine mammography and/or breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Objective To compare screening outcomes of breast MRI vs mammography by advanced breast cancer risk and screening round. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study included women aged 40 to 74 years who had a screening MRI performed with or without a screening film, digital, or digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) mammogram within 12 months (MRI group) or a screening digital or DBT mammogram (mammography-only group) performed at breast imaging facilities participating in the Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium (BCSC) between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2021, and breast cancers diagnosed between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2022. Data analysis was performed from April 2025 to August 2026. Exposures MRI and mammography; advanced breast cancer risk score calculated using the BCSC advanced cancer risk model and categorized as low (0% to &amp;lt;0.172%), average (0.172% to &amp;lt;0.3797%), intermediate (0.3797% to &amp;lt;0.6582%), or higher (≥0.6582%). Main Outcomes and Measures Advanced (prognostic stage II or higher) and screen-detected early-stage (prognostic stage I) invasive cancer and false-positive biopsy recommendation rates per 1000 examinations adjusting for registry, examination year, age, race and ethnicity, family history, prior breast biopsy, and breast density. Results A total of 172 865 examinations performed in 105 532 women (median [IQR] age, 52 [46-59] years) were studied. After mammography, the intermediate to high vs low to average risk group had significantly higher advanced cancer (0.6 vs 0.3; difference, 0.4; 95% CI, 0.1-0.6), screen-detected early-stage cancer (2.8 vs 1.8; difference, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.5-1.7), and false-positive biopsy recommendation (18.1 vs 14.7; difference, 3.4; 95% CI, 1.7-5.2) rates per 1000 examinations. In the MRI group, rates per 1000 examinations of advanced cancer (0.8 vs 1.1; difference, −0.3; 95% CI, −1.3 to 0.7), screen-detected early-stage disease (10.3 vs 11.4; difference, −1.1; 95% CI, −4.9 to 2.7), and false-positive biopsy recommendation (94.0 vs 93.3; difference, 0.7; 95% CI, −9.9 to 11.3) were not significantly different between intermediate to high and low to average advanced cancer risk groups. Advanced cancer rates were not significantly different for MRI vs mammography between risk groups (difference, 0.6; 95% CI, −0.4 to 1.6). Screen-detected early-stage rates were significantly higher for MRI vs mammography for low to average risk (11.4 vs 1.8; difference, 9.6; 95% CI, 7.3-12.0) and intermediate to high risk (10.3 vs 2.8; difference, 7.5; 95% CI, 4.9-10.1) groups as were false-positive biopsy recommendation rates for low to average risk (93.3 vs 14.7; difference, 78.6; 95% CI, 72.5-84.8) and intermediate to high risk (94.0 vs 18.1; difference, 75.9; 95% CI, 68.3-83.5) groups. Women who underwent subsequent vs first MRIs had significantly lower advanced cancer rates (0.4 vs 2.0; difference, 1.6; 95% CI, 0.3-2.8) and higher advanced cancer risk (median [IQR] BCSC advanced cancer risk score, 0.348 [0.238 to 0.490] vs 0.301 [0.213 to 0.429]; P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, intermediate to high advanced breast cancer risk was associated with higher advanced cancer rates with screening mammography. MRI screening was associated with higher screen-detected early-stage cancer rates compared with mammography but not lower advanced cancer rates, except among women who underwent repeat MRIs. These results suggest that women with elevated advanced cancer risk should discuss MRI screening with their physician.

item.title: Indoor Radon and Incident Heart Failure Among Postmenopausal Women
item.dc:creator: Shu Chen
Cuiran Shi
Jason M. Collins
Ayesha K. Ekanayaka
Carson Mowrer
James D. Stewart
David Y. Huang
Matthew A. Allison
item.description:
Authors: Shu Chen, Cuiran Shi, Jason M. Collins, Ayesha K. Ekanayaka, Carson Mowrer, James D. Stewart, David Y. Huang, Matthew A. Allison, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642391
Abstract: Importance Evidence has shown an association of radon exposure with heart failure risk factors, but whether there is an association with heart failure remains unclear. Objective To assess whether indoor radon concentrations are associated with incident heart failure among US postmenopausal women. Design, Setting, and Participants This prospective cohort study used data from the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) observational study and clinical trials. Participants were postmenopausal women from 40 US clinical centers who were aged 50 to 79 years and did not have self-reported heart failure at enrollment or randomization (September 1993 to December 1998) but had physician adjudication of heart failure during follow-up through February 17, 2024. Exposure Geocoded participant address–based assignment of county-level, US Environmental Protection Agency–categorized indoor radon concentration (&amp;lt;2, 2-4, or &amp;gt;4 picocuries [pCi]/L). Main Outcome and Measure Incident hospitalization for acute decompensated heart failure was ascertained through physician adjudication of medical records. Hazard ratios (HRs) for heart failure by indoor radon concentration were estimated with Cox proportional hazards regression models. Results Among 43 188 postmenopausal women (mean [SD] age, 63 [7] years), 36% were exposed to a radon concentration less than 2 pCi/L; 41%, to a concentration of 2 to 4 pCi/L; and 23%, to a concentration of more than 4 pCi/L. Over a mean (SD) follow-up of 16.2 (8.4) years, 3446 incident heart failure events occurred. The fully adjusted HR for heart failure was 1.19 (95% CI, 1.07-1.33) at more than 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L, changing little in sensitivity analyses. The HR was higher for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (1.24; 95% CI, 1.04-1.49) and heart failure mortality (1.37; 95% CI, 1.12-1.69) at radon concentrations more than 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L, but these HRs were not different from the null at concentrations of 2 to 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L. The HR at concentrations greater than 4 pCi/L approximated that of a 16–mm Hg increase in systolic blood pressure or an increase of 4.8 in body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of US postmenopausal women, higher indoor radon concentrations were associated with an increased risk of incident heart failure, suggesting that radon may be a modifiable environmental determinant of heart failure.

item.title: Distribution of Coal Power, Pollution, and Poverty
item.dc:creator: Eleanna M. Melcher
William R. Buckingham
Sarah A. Keller
Amy J. H. Kind
item.description:
Authors: Eleanna M. Melcher, William R. Buckingham, Sarah A. Keller, Amy J. H. Kind
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642335
Abstract: Importance The adverse social exposome—life-course exposure to harmful social-environmental conditions—is associated with poor health outcomes. Exposure to heavy metals in air pollution from coal-fired power plants (CPP) may represent an underlying mechanism of this disparity, yet the association between the US adverse social exposome measured with the Area Deprivation Index (ADI) and CPP remains unknown. Objective To characterize the populations and adverse social exposome (indexed by ADI) of communities neighboring operational CPP. Design, Setting, and Participants Cross-sectional study of the US population using data from the 2023 Neighborhood Atlas. Data were analyzed from March to April 2026. Exposure Proximity to CPP was operationalized using 4 circular buffer zones: 3, 10, 25, and 50 miles in radius. Main Outcomes and Measures (1) Characterize each buffer zone by ADI and (2) determine the potential population-level exposure to CPP. Census block group delineations and population characteristics are from time-concordant US Census and American Community Survey data. Results The 2023 US population included 335 563 144 people (169 517 541 [50.5%] female, 66 294 296 [19.8%] Hispanic, 269 268 846 [80.2%] not Hispanic or Latino, and 212 002 396 [63.1%] White). A total of 2 783 004 people (0.83% of the US population) lived within 3 miles of a CPP. This group was more likely to live in the highest ADI neighborhoods as compared with the lowest ADI neighborhoods. Compared with the US population, these individuals were more likely to be American Indian and Alaska Native, White, and non-Hispanic. Populations living in the lowest 10% of ADI neighborhoods (most advantaged) had lower odds (odds ratio, 0.04; 95% CI, 0.00-0.81) of living within 3 miles of a CPP as compared with populations living in the highest 10% of ADI neighborhoods (most disadvantaged). Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of US communities’ proximity to CPP, we found that neighborhoods potentially exposed to CPP’s hazardous environmental toxicants were more likely to be high ADI (ie, lower socioeconomic status) than low ADI (ie, higher socioeconomic status), highlighting the significantly greater burden of environmental toxicants potentially borne by disadvantaged US populations. Recent federal deregulations are likely to further increase these potential CPP-related toxin exposures. Additional study is needed to determine if these environmental toxicants trigger biological mechanisms underpinning the association between high ADI and poor health.

Authors: Laurent G. Glance, Andrew W. Dick, Eeshwar K. Chandrasekar, Donald E. Arnold, Andres F. Laserna, Heather L. Lander, Sonia G. Pyne, Julie A. Wyrobek, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642377
Abstract: Importance Understanding how racial-, ethnic-, and gender-based differences in academic promotion have changed over time is important for advancing equity in academic medicine. Objective To examine changes over time in racial-, ethnic-, and gender-based differences in promotion and attrition among academic clinical faculty. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used deidentified data from the AAMC faculty roster for full-time faculty appointments between 1960 and 2024, based on an August 31, 2025, data snapshot. Exposure Race and ethnicity (categorized as American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander; Asian; Black; Hispanic; White; and other [any race or ethnicity not otherwise specified]), gender, and medical school graduation cohort (2000 or earlier vs after 2000). Main Outcomes and Measures Cox proportional hazards models were used to examine differences in promotion to associate professor, professor, and attrition by race, ethnicity, and gender across medical school graduation cohorts and were presented as adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs). Results Included were 289 129 physicians at 152 institutions (179 081 men [61.9%]; 1093 American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander [0.4%]; 62 403 Asian [21.6%]; 13 330 Black [4.6%]; 16 865 Hispanic [5.8%]; 3034 other [1.1%]; 192 404 White [66.6%]). Compared with White faculty, Black faculty were less likely to be promoted to associate professor overall; this difference narrowed over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.60-0.74; after 2000: aHR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.71-0.83; P for interaction = .01). The difference in promotion to professor between Black and White faculty also narrowed over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.77-0.94; after 2000: aHR, 1.09, 95% CI, 0.92-1.29; P for interaction = .02). Women were less likely than men to be promoted to associate professor, although this difference narrowed over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.77-0.82; after 2000: aHR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.85-0.98; P for interaction &amp;lt;.001). Women were less likely than men to be promoted to professor in both graduation cohorts, with no evidence of change over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.97; after 2000: aHR 0.91; 95% CI, 0.83-0.99; P for interaction = .48). Attrition was more likely among American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander (aHR, 1.25; 95% CI, 1.12-1.40), Asian (aHR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.04-1.10), Black (aHR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.14-1.25), Hispanic (aHR, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.05-1.15), and women (aHR, 1.11; 95% CI: 1.08-1.13) faculty than among White and men faculty. Conclusions And Relevance In this retrospective cohort study of 289 129 physicians, Black faculty experienced less disparity in promotion over time, and disparities in promotion to associate professor also narrowed for women; however, women remained less likely to be promoted to professor, and attrition remained higher for all minoritized racial and ethnic groups and for women. These findings suggest incremental progress while underscoring the need for continued efforts to achieve greater diversity and equity within academic medicine.

item.dc:creator: Sarah Revak

item.description:
Authors: Sarah Revak, Senbagam Virudachalam, Christina A. Roberto, Justine Shults, Diana Montoya-Williams, DanaRose Negro, Aditi Vasan
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642161
Abstract: Importance Children who receive free or reduced-price school meals often face increased hunger during the summer, when school-based meals are unavailable. Since 2024, states may opt into implementing the Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer (SEBT) program, which provides low-income families a one-time, federally funded grocery benefit of $120 per school-aged child. Objective To examine the association between state implementation of SEBT and subsequent household food insufficiency among SEBT-eligible, low-income households with school-aged children. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study used demographic and health data from January to September 2024 cycles of the nationally representative Household Pulse Survey conducted by the US Census Bureau. Eligible households included children aged 5 to 17 years who were eligible for SEBT based on reported Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) receipt and/or income 185% of the federal poverty level (FPL) or below. Data analysis was performed between April 2025 and August 2026. Exposure State-level implementation of SEBT between May and August 2024 (treated vs untreated states). Main Outcomes and Measures Household food insufficiency, measured by a respondent indicating they sometimes or often did not have enough food in their household during the previous 7 days. Results Among 31 059 SEBT-eligible households (1090 Asian [3.5%], 5692 Black [18.3%], 5845 Hispanic [18.8%], 21 166 White [68.1%]), the majority of households in both untreated (18 states) and treated (33 states, including District of Columbia) states had income below 185% FPL (10 233 [93.4%] and 17 105 [92.0%], respectively). Among 11 334 households in untreated states, 4392 received Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) (42.6%) and 1196 received Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) benefits (12.3%); among 19 725 households in treated states, 9512 (50.4%) received SNAP, and 2126 (12.3%) received WIC. Among low-income families (185% FPL or below) with school-aged children, household food insufficiency increased by 4.0 percentage points (95% CI, 2.1 to 5.9 percentage points) during the summer compared with nonsummer months. Only a mean (SD) 30.3% (8.3) of SEBT-eligible households in treated states reported receiving SEBT. State implementation of SEBT was not significantly associated with a change in food insufficiency among SEBT-eligible households (0.8 percentage points; 95% CI, −2.4 to 4.0 percentage points). Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study, household food insufficiency increased significantly during summer months among low-income households of school-aged children and state implementation of SEBT was not significantly associated with a change in food insufficiency among SEBT-eligible households.

item.title: US Medical Education Reform Reports, 1910 to 2024
item.dc:creator: William C. McGaghie
Krystal L. Madkins
item.description:
Authors: William C. McGaghie, Krystal L. Madkins
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642347
Abstract: Importance Since the early 20th century, prominent private foundations, medical organizations, and government agencies have published reports calling for reform of medical education; however, it is unclear whether these reports contain repetitive messages about improving medical education, are a source of curriculum improvement, and are an antidote to medical education inertia. Objective To replicate and amplify findings of a similar analysis of reports published between 1910 and 1993 that advocated for reform in medical education using reports published from 1995 to 2024 and to identify recurring themes and potential sources of inertia in medical education. Evidence Review PubMed, Scopus, Education Resources Information Center, and Google were searched on February 4, February 13, and March 19, 2025, using search terms addressing medical education, reform, and recommendations to identify reports on reform in medical education. A descriptive and interpretive content analysis of the medical education reports spanning 114 years was conducted from February 2025 to May 2026. Findings A total of 47 reports, including 19 analyzed in the previous study, were identified and analyzed. Consistent coding of content in the 47 reports was achieved. One of 4 core reform objectives of medical education, serve changing public interest, increased in endorsement over time. The other 3 core objectives—address physician workforce needs, cope with burgeoning knowledge, foster generalism—decreased or were unchanged. Four secondary reform objectives—apply new educational methods, address the changing nature of illness burden, address the changing nature of practice, increase quality and standards of education—increased in prevalence. Proposed methods of educational reform varied over 114 years, shaped by conceptual updates and technology advancements. None of the reports expressed criticism of traditional apprenticeship clinical education. Few reports displayed knowledge or awareness of the science of expertise in medical education. Conclusions and Relevance In this study of medical education reports issued over 114 years, 3 basic values emerged: reform medical education, affirm core social and professional values, and protect the profession from outside intrusion. Proposed reform objectives and the means to achieve them displayed both stability and change longitudinally. The time-honored apprenticeship approach to clinical education was unquestioned. Despite a growing body of evidence from the science of expertise, proposed medical education reforms have produced insignificant curriculum change.

item.title: Molecular Testing Among Patients With Advanced Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer in the Rural US
item.dc:creator: Dena P. Rhinehart
Evelien van Gelderen
Josephine Feliciano
Craig Evan Pollack
Kristen A. Marrone
Amanda L. Blackford
item.description:
Authors: Dena P. Rhinehart, Evelien van Gelderen, Josephine Feliciano, Craig Evan Pollack, Kristen A. Marrone, Amanda L. Blackford
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642270
Abstract: Importance Molecular evaluation is standard of care for patients with advanced non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in the US. Patients in rural areas face disproportionate lung cancer mortality associated with reduced guideline-concordant evaluation and treatment receipt, but molecular testing patterns have not been described in this population. Objective To characterize molecular testing patterns in the rural US following initial testing implementation. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program linked to Medicare claims data to identify individuals aged 66 years or older diagnosed with advanced NSCLC from January 2014 to December 2019. Data analysis was performed from December 2025 to August 2026. Exposures Sociodemographic variables, histology, and practitioner visits. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was receipt of molecular testing. The cumulative incidence of testing overall and by patient subgroups defined at baseline were calculated using the total person-time at risk (30 days before diagnosis to death or 6 months after diagnosis) using a competing-risks framework, with death as the competing event. Results Among a total of 8259 Medicare beneficiaries residing in rural areas who were diagnosed with advanced NSCLC included in the study (mean [SD] age, 76.1 [6.7] years; 4672 males [56.6%]), 1775 (21.5%) were eligible for Medicaid, 3754 (45.5%) had adenocarcinoma histology, 2044 (24.7%) had squamous histology, and 2461 (29.8%) had other or unspecified histology. In the cohort, 2963 (35.9%) received molecular testing. The cumulative incidence of testing by 180 days after diagnosis was 0.36 (95% CI, 0.35-0.37). Increasing age (hazard ratio [HR], 0.96 [95% CI, 0.93-0.99]), later diagnosis year (HR, 1.05 [95% CI, 1.02-1.07]), dual Medicaid coverage (HR, 0.71 [95% CI, 0.64-0.79]), Part D enrollment (HR, 1.13 [95% CI, 1.04-1.22]), and squamous histology (HR, 0.35 [95% CI, 0.32-0.39]) were independently associated with testing. A greater percentage of patients who received testing had visits with both a proceduralist or a surgeon and an oncologist compared with those without testing (1257 [77.7%] vs 867 [58.9%]; P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of Medicare beneficiaries with advanced NSCLC residing in the rural US, initial receipt of molecular testing was low. Dual Medicaid coverage, Part D enrollment, and subspecialist visits were independently associated with test receipt, highlighting key areas for future study to promote equitable delivery of guideline-concordant lung cancer care.

item.description:
Authors: Joseph I. Friedman, Prathamesh Parchure, Weijia Fu, Satyanarayana Cheertirala, Prem Timsina, Ganesh Raut, Katherine Reina, Josiane Joseph-Jimerson, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642142
Abstract: Importance Although external validation of machine learning (ML)-based delirium risk models is a key stage in the model development pipeline, few published reports exist. Moreover, ML-based delirium risk models commonly degrade in performance during external validation. Objective To examine the performance of a fusion multimodal with natural language processing (NLP) delirium risk stratification model in live clinical practice with cross-hospital external validation. Design, Setting, and Participants This quality improvement study evaluated live clinical deployment of the model among patients 60 years or older who were admitted to non–intensive care units at Mount Sinai Hospital (MSH), with external validation performed at Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital (MSM), from December 1, 2024, to December 31, 2025. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were performance of the risk stratification model, assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and monthly delirium detection rates. A 2 × 2 confusion matrix was created, and the 4 cells were used to calculate model performance metrics and compare associated diagnostic yield between premodel deployment and active model deployment periods. Results The overall sample included 33 095 admissions to non–intensive care units at MSM and MSH (mean [SD] age, 74.86 (9.22) years; 15 601 women [47.1%], 17 271 men [52.2%]). A total of 9020 MSM inpatient admissions were assigned a delirium risk score by the risk stratification model during live clinical operations and were compared to 21 186 MSH inpatient admissions that were assigned a risk score by the same model. Age at admission significantly differed between patients at MSM and MSH (MSM: median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years vs MSH: 72.62 [66.64-79.65] years; P &amp;lt; .001). Patients from MSM and MSH also significantly differed by sex, race and ethnicity, surgical vs medical primary diagnosis, length of stay, and dementia prevalence rate. Among 11 909 MSM patients, patients in the pre-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 78.00 [71.00-85.00] years) were significantly older than those in the post-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years) ( P &amp;lt; .001). The AUROC of the model was 0.91 (95% CI, 0.90-0.92) for MSM and 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.94) for MSH. The positive predictive value of the model was 25.9% for MSM and 19.4% for MSH. For MSM, the mean monthly delirium detection rate significantly increased from 9.23% (95% CI, 8.07%-10.38%) to 19.59% (95% CI, 17.32%-21.85%) after model deployment ( P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this quality improvement study, an ML-based delirium risk stratification model maintained acceptable discriminative performance during external deployment without retraining and was similar to its performance at the development site without retraining. Model deployment was also associated with increased diagnostic yield but a high false positive rate. These findings provide further evidence of the potential generalizability of the model.
